title: Quantum Error Management In Practice: A Cross-Stack Benchmark
authors: Daniel Sierra-Sosa, Begonya Garcia-Zapirain, Cristian Marquez, Kelly Garces
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum processors have crossed the one-hundred-qubit mark, but noise continues to limit circuit performance, while full quantum error correction remains too costly for routine use. Error suppression and mitigation therefore play an important role in extracting value from current hardware, yet independent comparisons of commercial solutions on identical workloads and devices remain scarce. We benchmark IBM Qiskit Runtime, Q-CTRL Performance Management, and Qedma QESEM on IBM Pittsburgh, a 156-qubit IBM Quantum Heron r3 processor. For Sampler workloads, we run Bernstein-Vazirani, quantum phase estimation, GHZ-state preparation, and randomized mirror circuits with up to 100 measured qubits, comparing raw execution, IBM measurement twirling, and Q-CTRL. For Estimator workloads, we measure chain-averaged magnetization and correlation observables of an eight-layer transverse-field Ising circuit at 25, 50, and 75 qubits against an exact matrix-product-state reference, comparing IBM raw execution, IBM TREX plus twirling, Q-CTRL, and QESEM. Q-CTRL produced the best results on the three structured Sampler workloads while keeping reported QPU times within the same order as the IBM configurations. Across six Ising observable and system-size cases, aggregate mean absolute error was 0.0883 for IBM raw execution, 0.0807 for IBM TREX plus twirling, 0.0285 for Q-CTRL, and 0.0188 for QESEM. Relative to raw execution, Q-CTRL and QESEM reduced aggregate error by factors of 3.10 and 4.70, respectively, while QESEM used 7.5 to 11.1 times the reported QPU time of Q-CTRL. These results show that managed error suppression and mitigation can substantially improve current hardware performance, but with distinct accuracy and execution-time tradeoffs.
tldr: This paper benchmarks commercial quantum error suppression and mitigation tools on IBM quantum hardware, comparing their accuracy and execution time across various workloads.
motivation: Quantum processors are noisy, and full error correction is impractical; thus, error suppression and mitigation are essential for practical use, but independent comparisons of commercial solutions are scarce.
method: The authors benchmark IBM Qiskit Runtime, Q-CTRL Performance Management, and Qedma QESEM on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor, running Sampler and Estimator workloads with up to 100 qubits, and compare raw execution, twirling, and mitigation techniques.
result: Q-CTRL performed best on structured Sampler workloads, while QESEM achieved the lowest aggregate error on Ising observables (0.0188 vs 0.0883 raw), but used 7.5-11.1x more QPU time than Q-CTRL.
conclusion: Managed error suppression and mitigation can significantly improve hardware performance, but there are distinct trade-offs between accuracy and execution time.

title: One Qubit Can Beat One Bit: Quantum Advantage For Post-Training Quantization
authors: Moeto Mishima Yuma Ichikawa
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One-bit post-training quantization represents each weight using only its sign, requiring all deployment contexts to share the same binary weight matrix even when their activation statistics favor different sign patterns. We study this shared-sign constraint and introduce Quantum Random Access Quantization (QRAQ). This framework encodes context-dependent signs in a quantum random-access code and retrieves them via context-matched Pauli measurements. Under an explicit fresh-copy logical readout model, QRAQ produces an unbiased, context-specific binary surrogate with a tractable shot-noise penalty. We prove a row-wise separation from shared-sign one-bit PTQ with signed per-row scales. When the optimal context-wise signs are incompatible, QRAQ achieves a strictly lower ideal reconstruction risk. We also derive finite-shot and calibrated-noise conditions under which this separation is retained. Fixed-readout quantum schemes are classically simulable, so the relevant resource in this model is measurement incompatibility rather than quantization alone. Finally, we characterize the role of scale granularity, provide finite-sample certificates, and evaluate the predicted ideal, finite-shot, noisy, and multi-context regimes in simulator experiments.
tldr: This paper introduces a quantum-inspired method for post-training quantization of neural networks, using quantum random access codes to encode context-dependent signs, but it is not related to the user's research interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The paper addresses a practical machine learning problem: improving one-bit post-training quantization by allowing context-dependent sign patterns, which is not aligned with the user's focus on fundamental quantum information and thermodynamics.
method: The authors propose Quantum Random Access Quantization (QRAQ), which encodes context-dependent signs in a quantum random-access code and retrieves them via Pauli measurements, with a fresh-copy logical readout model.
result: They prove a row-wise separation from shared-sign one-bit PTQ, showing lower ideal reconstruction risk when context-wise signs are incompatible, and provide finite-shot and noise conditions for this advantage.
conclusion: The paper concludes that measurement incompatibility is the key resource, and the advantage is retained under certain conditions, but the work is primarily a machine learning application with no clear connection to the user's research areas.

title: Transparent Boundary Conditions For The Spatially Discrete Schr\"odinger Equation: Reflectionless Quantum Transport In 1d Lattices
authors: Mashrab E. Akramov, Jambul R. Yusupov, Matthias Ehrhardt, Davron U. Matrasulov
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct exact transparent boundary conditions (TBCs) for a time-continuous, spatially discrete Schr\"odinger equation that models a one-dimensional quantum lattice. Using a recently developed exact solution for the discrete system, we derive the Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps analytically via Laplace transforms. This yields a convolution-type boundary condition governed by Bessel functions. We rigorously demonstrate the consistency of this discrete formulation with its continuous counterpart in the continuum limit. Additionally, we present an efficient time-discretization scheme based on the trapezoidal rule for practical implementation. Numerical experiments using a Crank-Nicolson solver verify that our proposed TBCs eliminate spurious backscattering entirely and preserve reflectionless propagation of a Gaussian wave packet exiting the computational domain.
tldr: This paper derives exact transparent boundary conditions for a discrete Schrödinger equation on a 1D lattice, focusing on numerical simulation of quantum transport without backscattering.
motivation: To enable efficient and accurate numerical simulations of quantum transport on lattices by eliminating spurious reflections at computational boundaries.
method: The authors use Laplace transforms and the exact solution of the discrete Schrödinger equation to derive Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps, resulting in convolution-type boundary conditions with Bessel functions. They also propose a trapezoidal rule time-discretization and implement a Crank-Nicolson solver.
result: Numerical experiments show that the proposed transparent boundary conditions completely eliminate spurious backscattering and preserve reflectionless propagation of Gaussian wave packets.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous and practical method for implementing transparent boundary conditions in discrete quantum lattice simulations, with consistency to the continuous limit.

title: Feasibility-Preserving Quantum Search For Constrained Transportation Routing
authors: Monika Filipovska Dahye Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transportation routing problems such as the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) are characterized by strict feasibility requirements involving customer assignment and visit rules, route sequencing, and depot-return logic alongside cost minimization. Most quantum routing formulations adopt Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) encodings, where feasibility is incorporated indirectly via penalty terms in the cost Hamiltonian. While convenient for standard implementations of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), QUBO encodings allow the quantum search dynamics to allocate substantial probability to infeasible route configurations. This study develops a transportation-grounded constraint-aware Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA+) framework that embeds feasibility-preserving logic directly into the search operator. We introduce a custom mixer that functions as a quantum analogue of feasibility-preserving routing neighborhoods, using column-wise swap moves, it restricts evolution to feasible configurations while enabling structured exploration of valid routes. We compare three constraint-handling architectures: penalty-based QUBO QAOA, penalty free QAOA+ with the feasibility-preserving mixer, and a Hybrid QAOA+ combining mixer based feasibility with and penalty guidance. Results on small TSP and VRP instances show that constraint-handling architecture strongly influences feasible-route sampling, convergence behavior, and probability concentration over low-cost feasible routes. These findings position constraint-aware quantum search as a methodological extension of transportation routing search approaches, where feasibility is enforced through admissible quantum transitions rather than post-hoc penalties.
tldr: This paper proposes a feasibility-preserving quantum search framework for constrained transportation routing using QAOA+ with custom mixers.
motivation: To address the issue of infeasible solutions in QUBO-based quantum routing formulations by embedding feasibility constraints directly into the quantum search operator.
method: Introduces a QAOA+ framework with a custom mixer that performs column-wise swap moves to restrict evolution to feasible route configurations, and compares penalty-based QUBO QAOA, penalty-free QAOA+, and a hybrid approach.
result: On small TSP and VRP instances, the constraint-handling architecture significantly affects feasible-route sampling, convergence, and probability concentration over low-cost feasible routes.
conclusion: Constraint-aware quantum search can enforce feasibility through admissible quantum transitions, offering a methodological extension for transportation routing.

title: Interferometric Quantum Polynomial Chaos Expansion As A Generative Model For Calorimeter Shower Simulation
authors: Jamal Slim, Saverio Monaco, Florian Rehm, Dirk Kruecker, Frank Gaede, Kerstin Borras
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the quantum polynomial chaos expansion, a generative algorithm in which a single circuit is the entire model, and we use it to learn calorimeter images. In a classical chaos expansion the randomness is the input and the coefficients are fitted. Here the randomness is still the only input, entering the circuit as rotation angles and re-uploaded at every block, so that each measured observable is a chaos expansion of the latent variables whose order equals the circuit depth, and what is fitted are the gate angles themselves. Expressivity therefore grows with depth rather than with classical coefficients, correlations between outputs arise only from entangling gates, and a single latent wire read by all qubits carries the collective mode of the data. Nothing fitted stands between the circuit and the sample, so switching the entanglers off is a setting of the model itself and provably yields independent outputs, and attribution of the learned correlations to individual gates becomes a measurement. Choosing between two measurement bases shot by shot sharpens attribution into certification, and the trained model violates the Bell bound obeyed by every classical generative model with local response, whatever its size. We train the model on Geant4 shower data, execute the identical circuit on a superconducting processor with its accuracy loss predicted in advance, prove a no-go theorem for the tail dependence of every smooth generator read out through expectation values, and identify the circuit primitive that removes this limit.
tldr: This paper introduces a quantum generative model based on polynomial chaos expansion for simulating calorimeter showers, but it does not align with the specified research directions.
motivation: The authors aim to leverage quantum computing for high-energy physics simulation, specifically to generate calorimeter images efficiently.
method: They propose a quantum polynomial chaos expansion where a single parameterized quantum circuit acts as the generative model, with randomness encoded as rotation angles and re-uploaded at each block, and gate angles fitted to data.
result: The model is trained on Geant4 shower data, executed on a superconducting processor, and demonstrates that it can violate Bell bounds, indicating non-classical correlations, while also addressing tail dependence limitations.
conclusion: The work presents a novel quantum generative approach for calorimeter simulation, but it is primarily an application in high-energy physics and quantum machine learning, not directly contributing to the user's core interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Data-driven Reconstruction Of Dynamical Systems Using Takens' Theorem, Manifold Learning, And Universal Function Approximators
authors: Andrew L. Ferguson Maximilian Topel
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedding theorems can be used to provide theoretical guarantees about the relation between low-dimensional observations of a system and its full-dimensional state and dynamics. Such theorems do not, however, provide guidance on observable choice, embedding construction, or methodologies to learn the mapping between the embedding and full-dimensional state. In this work, we develop an algorithmic framework, TAkens Reconstruction (TAR), to analyze and reconstruct arbitrary dynamical systems from low-dimensional time series using an integration of Takens' Delay Embedding Theorem, manifold learning techniques, and universal function approximators. We validate TAR in applications to a variety of simulated and observed dynamical systems and use it to investigate how delay vector structure impacts reconstruction accuracy. In an ecological system, we show that simple predator-prey dynamics can be reconstructed with observations taken over a wide variety of embedding time scales. In molecular dynamics simulations of the protein Villin, we demonstrate how including multiple time delays of the same observable series can be used to improve reconstruction of systems with multiple characteristic time scales. In the trade record of Vanguard S&P 500, we show how the approach exposes underlying dynamical phenomenologies in the data and accurate return predictions over short time horizons without access to full-dimensional market observations. We develop and release an open-source software package to enable the application of TAR to arbitrary dynamical systems.
tldr: This paper develops a data-driven framework (TAR) for reconstructing dynamical systems from time series using Takens' theorem, manifold learning, and universal function approximators.
motivation: The authors aim to provide practical methods for reconstructing full-dimensional dynamics from low-dimensional observations, addressing the gap between theoretical embedding theorems and practical implementation.
method: They integrate Takens' delay embedding, manifold learning (e.g., diffusion maps), and universal function approximators (e.g., neural networks) to learn the mapping from delay vectors to the full state space.
result: The method is validated on simulated and real systems, including predator-prey dynamics, protein folding (Villin), and financial time series, showing accurate reconstruction and prediction.
conclusion: The framework offers a general, open-source tool for dynamical system reconstruction from time series, with potential applications across various fields.

title: Morphology Of Frozen Labyrinths From Irreversible Threshold Dynamics
authors: Daniel Richard Levy
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Majority threshold dynamics, in which each agent adopts the dominant state in a weighted neighborhood, relaxes a binary field toward consensus or stripes. We study what happens when this rule is made irreversible: each agent, interacting through a Gaussian kernel on a lattice, may flip out of its local weighted minority at most once. The reversible form is threshold dynamics of Merriman-Bence-Osher type, an exactly solvable calibration in which interfaces move by mean curvature with closed-form lattice pinning and mobility. Irreversibility changes the outcome. From random initial conditions, the one-flip rule freezes balanced non-consensus labyrinths that reversible relaxation drives away. The patterned regime is a window of initial spin compositions around equal balance, narrowing as the interaction range grows, controlled by a standardized bias whose onset is independent of scale over a fourfold range. The frozen morphology is arrested coarsening: bicontinuous at balance, with a feature width that grows sublinearly and falls below the interaction range at large scales. We determine the mechanism by intervention. Fixing the initial condition while varying the update order shows that the coarse domain layout is deterministic, while the update order enters only in a secondary first-passage race that fine-tunes the wall positions the deterministic dynamics has already set. Those walls are marked by frustration: agents frozen against their own local field. This signature is identically absent from any reversible relaxation, is overwhelmingly interfacial, and carries almost none of the pattern's large-scale shape.
tldr: This paper studies irreversible majority threshold dynamics on lattices, revealing frozen labyrinthine patterns and arrested coarsening, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the effect of irreversibility on threshold dynamics, which typically relax to consensus or stripes, and to characterize the resulting frozen patterns.
method: They simulate a one-flip rule on a lattice with Gaussian kernel, varying initial spin compositions and update orders, and analyze the morphology and scaling of the frozen patterns.
result: They find a window of initial compositions around balance that freezes into bicontinuous labyrinths, with feature width growing sublinearly and update order only fine-tuning wall positions.
conclusion: The frozen morphology is determined by deterministic dynamics, with frustration marking interfaces, and the phenomenon is scale-invariant over a fourfold range.

title: Large Anomalous Shifts Of Potassium-39 Feshbach Resonances
authors: Ali Zaheer, Mohammed Bouras, Krzysztof Giergiel, Rudolf Grimm, Andrei Sidorov, Peter Hannaford
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the observation of large anomalous shifts, up to +7.5 G, of the positions of the 33.6 G and 39.9 G Feshbach resonances in potassium-39 atoms confined in a 1063.9 nm optical dipole trap (ODT) at temperatures up to around 35 {\mu}K and trap depths up to about 136 {\mu}K. When the atom cloud is cooled to lower temperatures, by reducing the trap depth of the ODT, the shifts decrease proportionally with trap depth and approach zero at zero depth. We show that the large observed shifts originate from a large differential ac Stark shift between the incoming pair of potassium-39 atoms and the weakly bound Feshbach molecule, which in turn originates from an unexpectedly large dynamic polarizability of the Feshbach molecule. The polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules extracted from the measured shifts of the 33.6 G and 39.9 G resonances are about four to seven times the sum of the polarizabilities of the two incoming potassium-39 atoms, that is, about four to seven times larger than the usual polarizability of weakly bound Feshbach molecules. The large polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules are attributed to a near-coincidence between the frequency of the 1063.9 nm ODT laser and the frequency of a molecular transition from the last vibrational level of the lowest triplet a3{\Sigma}+u potential to a vibrational level of the excited b3{\Sigma}+g potential. Other potassium-39 Feshbach resonances we have studied exhibit a zero or very small shift, corresponding to molecular polarizabilities close to the sum of the polarizabilities of the two incoming potassium-39 atoms.
tldr: This paper reports large anomalous shifts of potassium-39 Feshbach resonances in an optical dipole trap, attributed to enhanced molecular polarizability due to a near-resonant transition.
motivation: Understanding and controlling Feshbach resonances is crucial for ultracold atom experiments, but the observed shifts are anomalously large and need explanation.
method: The authors measure resonance positions as a function of trap depth and temperature, and model the shifts using differential ac Stark shifts and molecular polarizabilities.
result: They find shifts up to +7.5 G, with molecular polarizabilities four to seven times larger than expected, due to a near-coincidence with a molecular transition.
conclusion: The large shifts arise from enhanced polarizability of Feshbach molecules, which must be accounted for in precision experiments.

title: Dual-polarization Control Of Broadband Nonreciprocal Thermal Radiation By Combining Local And Nonlocal Metasurfaces
authors: Shuang Xia, Mengqi Liu, Wenjian Wan, Jialong Wang, Weihao Yang, Chaoran Wang, Huiqin Ma, Jun Qin, Hua Li, Yuan Wang, Lei Bi, Chengwei Qiu, Xiaobo Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonreciprocal thermal radiation offers a route to decouple spectral directional absorptivity and emissivity, thereby enabling new paradigms in thermal-photonic systems. However, in magneto-optical platforms, the intrinsic gyroelectric response generally confines observable nonreciprocity to transverse-magnetic (TM) polarization, while the transverse-electric (TE) response is absent. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate, for the first time, a local thermal metasurface strategy to activate TE-polarized nonreciprocity by creating artificial gyromagnetic response in a gyroelectric semiconductor platform. We further extend this mechanism to broadband dual-polarization operation employing a nonlocal thermal metasurface, which combines a resonator supercell with gradient-doped epsilon-near-zero magneto-optical multilayers. Pronounced absorptivity contrast is maintained over 22-27 {\mu}m for TE polarization and 19-27 {\mu}m for TM polarization. This platform provides a mechanism-based route to achieve broadband and dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal absorption, opening new opportunities for advancing radiative energy-conversion devices.
tldr: This paper experimentally demonstrates dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal radiation using local and nonlocal metasurfaces on a magneto-optical platform.
motivation: To overcome the limitation of nonreciprocal thermal radiation being confined to TM polarization in magneto-optical platforms, enabling TE-polarized nonreciprocity and broadband dual-polarization operation.
method: The authors design a local thermal metasurface to create artificial gyromagnetic response in a gyroelectric semiconductor, and extend it to a nonlocal metasurface combining a resonator supercell with gradient-doped epsilon-near-zero magneto-optical multilayers.
result: They achieve pronounced absorptivity contrast over 22-27 μm for TE polarization and 19-27 μm for TM polarization, demonstrating broadband dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal absorption.
conclusion: This work provides a mechanism-based route to achieve broadband and dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal absorption, advancing radiative energy-conversion devices.

title: Spectrally Flat And Broadband Doublepumped Fiber Optical Parametric Amplifiers
authors: J. M. Chavez Boggio, J. D. Marconi, S. R. Bickham, H. L. Fragnito
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study theoretically and experimentally spectrally flat and broadband double-pumped fiber-optical parametric amplifiers (2P-FOPAs). Closed formulas are derived for the gain ripple in 2P-FOPAs as a function of the pump wavelength separation and power, and the fiber non-linearity and fourth order dispersion coefficients. The impact of longitudinal random variations of the zero dispersion wavelength [MATH] on the gain flatness is investigated. Our theoretical findings are substantiated with experiments using conventional dispersion shifted fibers and highly nonlinear fibers (HNLFs). By using a HNLF having a low variation of [MATH] we demonstrate high gain and flat spectrum ([MATH]) over [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies spectrally flat and broadband double-pumped fiber optical parametric amplifiers, focusing on gain ripple and dispersion variations.
motivation: The authors aim to improve the performance of fiber optical parametric amplifiers for applications such as wavelength conversion and signal amplification.
method: They derive closed-form formulas for gain ripple and experimentally verify them using dispersion-shifted and highly nonlinear fibers, including effects of zero-dispersion wavelength variations.
result: They demonstrate high gain and flat spectrum over a broad bandwidth using a highly nonlinear fiber with low dispersion variation.
conclusion: The work provides design guidelines for achieving flat and broadband amplification in fiber parametric amplifiers.

title: Finite Quantum Histories: Holonomy Spectra, Minimal Clocks, And Exact Clock-Change Covariance
authors: Maxim V. Churilov
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve cyclic finite-dimensional quantum histories for arbitrary time-dependent unitary steps, without assuming that one step has finite order. The propagation Hamiltonian is a unitary connection Laplacian on a cycle; its complete gauge invariant is the monodromy [MATH]. Its spectrum is [MATH], where [MATH]. Thus the exact history sector is isomorphic to [MATH], while frustration, the gap above a nonempty zero-energy sector, the determinant, and the finite-temperature trace are obtained in closed form. Ordinary spectral data recover the multiset of monodromy phase cosines but not phase orientation; low energy certifies proximity to an exact relational history. We then define the predictive quotient of a sharp finite clock relative to an accessible operator system as the unique coarsest event alphabet preserving all conditional statistics on a history sector. A finite-error theorem shows that threshold clustering recovers this quotient when the minimum diamond separation of inequivalent event channels exceeds four times the estimation error, and proves an optimal record-count bound. With full matrix access and homogeneous step [MATH], the minimal number of clock events is the projective order of [MATH]. We distinguish the normalizer of the clock algebra from transformations preserving the coherent history code and classify oriented exact sharp clock changes by [MATH] on a rank-[MATH] history sector; without orientation the cyclic factor becomes dihedral. Reversible changes of full-information clock fibers are necessarily unitary, so irreversible coarse-graining is not exact clock covariance. Minimal realizations of a complete history Gram kernel are uniquely unitarily equivalent, with a finite-data Procrustes bound. Independent finite-matrix code verifies the main results.
tldr: This paper develops a mathematical framework for finite quantum histories, focusing on holonomy spectra, minimal clocks, and exact clock-change covariance.
motivation: The author aims to solve cyclic finite-dimensional quantum histories for arbitrary time-dependent unitary steps and to characterize the structure of quantum clocks and their transformations.
method: The paper uses unitary connection Laplacians on cycles, monodromy, spectral analysis, and algebraic classifications of clock algebras and event alphabets.
result: It provides closed-form expressions for the spectrum, frustration, and other quantities, and proves theorems about minimal clocks and the uniqueness of minimal realizations.
conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous mathematical foundation for finite quantum histories and clock covariance, but it is highly abstract and not directly connected to the user's specified research directions.

title: Transverse Quantum-state Characterization Of Programmable Electron Optics
authors: Shengbo You, Paolo Rosi, Enzo Rotunno, Alberto Roncaglia, Luca Belsito, Amir H. Tavabi, Rafal E. Dunin-Borkowski, Vincenzo Grillo, Philipp M. Pelz
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable electron optics -- electronically controlled phase plates -- underpin proposals from dose-efficient phase imaging to shaped-electron X-ray sources, nearly all assuming a pure, fully coherent delivered wave whose purity has never been measured. Here we reconstruct the transverse density matrix of a microelectromechanical electrostatic spiral phase plate by mixed-state ptychography, from one four-dimensional STEM scan per state and without added hardware. The delivered beam is substantially mixed: its purity falls from approximately 0.47 to approximately 0.24 as the applied bias grows, inconsistent with a fixed lateral source-blur model, while the real-space coherence width stays near 1 nm. The same scans calibrate the device in situ, allow virtual orbital-angular-momentum sorting and, through a partial-coherence-aware transfer theory, indicate that purifying the output could improve dose efficiency roughly threefold. One acquisition thus becomes a quantum-state acceptance test for programmable electron optics, supplying the purity and coherence that emerging phase-plate and diffractive-imaging schemes assume but leave unquantified.
tldr: This paper characterizes the transverse quantum state of programmable electron optics using mixed-state ptychography, revealing significant mixedness and coherence properties.
motivation: Programmable electron optics assume pure, coherent beams, but the actual purity has never been measured, which is critical for applications like dose-efficient phase imaging.
method: The authors reconstruct the transverse density matrix of a microelectromechanical electrostatic spiral phase plate using mixed-state ptychography from a single 4D-STEM scan per state, without additional hardware.
result: The beam purity decreases from ~0.47 to ~0.24 with increasing bias, and the real-space coherence width remains near 1 nm, inconsistent with a fixed lateral source-blur model. The scans also calibrate the device and enable virtual OAM sorting.
conclusion: The method provides a quantum-state acceptance test for programmable electron optics, indicating that purifying the output could improve dose efficiency roughly threefold.

title: Qsci-cmp: Quantum-Selected Configuration Interaction With Chemically Motivated Preselection
authors: Kosuke Mitarai Masahiko Kamoshita
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present QSCI-CMP, a quantum-classical hybrid algorithm for molecular ground-state calculations that reduces both the query count and the gate count of sample-based quantum diagonalization with amplitude amplification (SQD-AA). SQD-AA mitigates the measurement bottleneck of quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) by amplifying the basis states that have not yet been measured. Its oracle, however, specifies the measured states by listing them one by one, so its gate count grows with the number of collected states. Moreover, the quantum resources are spent even on states whose importance is evident from chemical knowledge, such as low-order excitations from the Hartree-Fock reference, which could be collected classically at the outset. We therefore propose to fix such chemically trivial states in advance, include them in the diagonalization subspace from the start, and exclude them from the amplification target, using a low-cost oracle that recognizes them through the excitation level and the seniority number of each basis state. We numerically demonstrate that QSCI-CMP reduces the query count and the gate count required to reach chemical accuracy by up to approximately 68% and 72% relative to SQD-AA for 24-qubit systems. The chemically trivial subspace is freely tunable within the classical computational budget. A larger subspace shifts more work onto the classical solver and increases the reduction in quantum cost, and when it captures the ground state sufficiently well, no quantum sampling is needed at all. We also point out that a query-optimal iteration count known from the analysis of quantum search further reduces the query count of both methods by approximately 12%.
tldr: This paper presents a quantum-classical hybrid algorithm for molecular ground-state calculations, focusing on reducing quantum resource usage in quantum-selected configuration interaction.
motivation: The authors aim to reduce the query and gate counts of sample-based quantum diagonalization with amplitude amplification (SQD-AA) for molecular simulations, which is a practical quantum chemistry problem.
method: They propose QSCI-CMP, which preselects chemically trivial states (low-order excitations) classically and excludes them from the amplification oracle, using a low-cost oracle based on excitation level and seniority number.
result: Numerical demonstrations on 24-qubit systems show up to ~68% reduction in query count and ~72% reduction in gate count compared to SQD-AA, with further ~12% reduction using query-optimal iteration count.
conclusion: The method effectively shifts computational work to classical resources, reducing quantum cost, and can eliminate quantum sampling when the classical subspace captures the ground state well.

title: Media Meets Communication In 6g: Fundamentals, Key Technologies, And Applications
authors: Bingyan Xie, Longyu Zhou, Zihan Chen, Shunpu Tang, Mingyang Shi, Yu Tian, Guo Lu, Yongpeng Wu, Tianhao Liang, Tony Q. S. Quek, Guangtao Zhai, Wenjun Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid advancement of sixth-generation (6G) networks is accelerating the convergence of media intelligence and communication intelligence, driving media communication beyond conventional bit-level delivery toward intelligent, semantic-aware, and generative paradigms. Emerging media services require not only high data rates and low latency, but also semantic awareness, perceptual quality assurance, adaptive resource orchestration, trustworthy content processing, and personalized media generation. Meanwhile, media technologies are evolving from handcrafted signal processing and conventional coding toward artificial intelligence (AI)-driven representation learning, content understanding, and generative reconstruction. Motivated by these trends, this paper presents a systematic survey of media communication technologies for 6G vision communication by revisiting the evolution of communication and media technologies and clarifying the intrinsic relationship between media content processing and wireless transmission. We introduce a unified framework consisting of four key dimensions: AI-driven media technologies, media-aware wireless transmission, large model-enabled media communication, and intelligent network infrastructures. Specifically, AI-driven media technologies encompass media coding, content understanding, quality assessment, security and compliance detection, and AIGC-enabled media generation, while media-aware wireless transmission is examined from three complementary perspectives: semantic joint source-channel optimization, which jointly encodes task-relevant semantic information; source-aware transmission optimization, which leverages media characteristics for channel adaptation, prediction, and compensation; and channel-aware source optimization, which adapts media coding and reconstruction based on real-time channel conditions.
tldr: This paper surveys media communication technologies for 6G networks, focusing on AI-driven media processing and wireless transmission integration.
motivation: The authors aim to address the convergence of media intelligence and communication intelligence in 6G, moving beyond conventional bit-level delivery to semantic-aware and generative paradigms.
method: The paper provides a systematic survey, proposing a unified framework with four dimensions: AI-driven media technologies, media-aware wireless transmission, large model-enabled media communication, and intelligent network infrastructures.
result: It reviews and categorizes existing technologies in media coding, content understanding, quality assessment, semantic joint source-channel optimization, and channel-aware source optimization.
conclusion: The paper concludes that integrating AI and semantic communication is essential for future 6G media services, but it does not present novel technical contributions.

title: Structured Tensor Approximation From Lateral Slice Sampling Via Basis And Manifold Priors
authors: Jeongmin Chae, Usama Saleem, Selin Bac, Shaama Mallikarjun Sharada, Urbashi Mitra
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we consider a structured tensor approximation problem, where only a limited number of lateral slices are observed. The proposed algorithm , called Basis and Manifold prior Tensor Approximation (BMTA), exploits both global and local structures of the evolution of a global tensor. Specifically, BMTA integrates two signal models: (i) a quasi-basis model that captures smooth global variations along a physical trajectory, and (ii) a manifold-guided interpolation model that characterizes local relationships among tensor slices. A low-rank Tucker reconstruction framework is incorporated to efficiently capture the priors, resulting in coefficients for basis function estimation and a tensor optimization. In addition, we provide a theoretical analysis which establishes a non-asymptotic reconstruction error bound that characterizes the effects of sampling complexity, optimization convergence, and model mismatch. Numerical experiments are performed on both synthetic and real-world datasets, including quantum chemistry and spatiotemporal sensing applications.
tldr: This paper proposes a tensor approximation algorithm using basis and manifold priors for lateral slice sampling, applied to quantum chemistry and spatiotemporal sensing.
motivation: The authors aim to reconstruct a global tensor from limited lateral slice observations by exploiting both global smooth variations and local relationships among slices.
method: The BMTA algorithm integrates a quasi-basis model and a manifold-guided interpolation model within a low-rank Tucker reconstruction framework, with theoretical non-asymptotic error bounds.
result: Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets (quantum chemistry, spatiotemporal sensing) demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.
conclusion: The method provides a principled way to approximate structured tensors from partial observations, with theoretical guarantees.

title: A Recentered-Domain Yau-Yau Filter For Target Tracking
authors: Lei Ma, Yuzhong Hu, Xiaoming Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Yau-Yau filter reformulates nonlinear state estimation as probability-density propagation governed by the Forward Kolmogorov equation (FKE). Applying it to target tracking, however, requires efficient FKE approximation on a finite computational domain. This paper proposes a Recentered-Domain Yau-Yau Filter (RD-YYF), which solves the FKE within a fixed-size local window centered at the latest state estimate. This design concentrates numerical resolution near the dominant posterior density. Offline, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) generate FKE solution snapshots, while principal component analysis constructs a low-dimensional representation of density evolution. A lightweight residual surrogate maps the initial-condition coefficients and domain center to the terminal-solution coefficients. Online, the pretrained surrogate predicts density evolution within the recentered window, followed by observation update and state estimation. Experiments on two geometrically constrained target-tracking examples show that RD-YYF achieves lower tracking errors than the extended Kalman filter (EKF) and particle filter (PF), while retaining efficient per-timestep inference. Ablation results indicate that domain recentering improves density approximation in high-probability regions and accelerates offline PINN convergence. These results demonstrate the potential of RD-YYF for efficient nonlinear target tracking.
tldr: This paper proposes a recentered-domain Yau-Yau filter for target tracking using physics-informed neural networks and principal component analysis.
motivation: The authors aim to improve nonlinear target tracking by efficiently approximating the Forward Kolmogorov equation on a finite domain.
method: The method solves the FKE in a fixed-size window centered on the latest estimate, using offline PINN snapshots and PCA for a low-dimensional surrogate, then online prediction and update.
result: Experiments show lower tracking errors than EKF and PF, with efficient inference, and ablation confirms benefits of recentering.
conclusion: The RD-YYF demonstrates potential for efficient nonlinear target tracking, but it is not related to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: An Ordered-Reliability-Bits Chase Decoding Algorithm For Bch Codes
authors: Wenwu Zhu, Min Zhu, Baoming Bai
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a low-complexity ordered-reliability-bits Chase (ORB-Chase) decoding algorithm for BCH codes. The proposed algorithm differs from the traditional Chase algorithm in two key aspects. First, it employs the logical weight as a metric to generate test error patterns (TEPs). Second, it introduces an integer-based early termination criterion that ensures computation can stop at the earliest possible stage if the maximum-likelihood codeword is identified, thereby minimizing unnecessary computational effort. Simulation results for (127, 113, 5) BCH codes and (256, 239, 6) eBCH codes demonstrate that the ORB-Chase algorithm achieves near-ML performance with significantly fewer test patterns compared to the Chase algorithm. Moreover, the average number of Berlekamp-Massey (BM) decoding calls decreases rapidly as [MATH] increases, achieving a reduction of up to 98.1% compared to the Chase algorithm at the same BLER performance.
tldr: This paper proposes a low-complexity ordered-reliability-bits Chase decoding algorithm for BCH codes, achieving near-ML performance with fewer test patterns.
motivation: The authors aim to reduce the computational complexity of Chase decoding for BCH codes while maintaining near-maximum-likelihood error performance.
method: The ORB-Chase algorithm uses logical weight to generate test error patterns and introduces an integer-based early termination criterion to stop decoding when the ML codeword is identified.
result: Simulations on (127,113,5) BCH and (256,239,6) eBCH codes show near-ML performance with significantly fewer test patterns and up to 98.1% reduction in average BM decoding calls.
conclusion: The proposed algorithm offers a practical low-complexity decoding solution for BCH codes, but it is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Annealed Ruelle-Pollicott Resonances
authors: Maxence Phalempin Sakshi Jain
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We adapt the theory of Ruelle-Pollicott resonances to annealed random dynamical systems generated by independent and identically distributed families of maps. Introducing annealed transfer and Koopman operators, we define resonances as elements of the point spectrum of the associated operators and establish a decorrelation formula relating these resonances to the asymptotic decay of annealed correlations. We then study several classes of systems for which the theory can be made explicit. First, we consider a family of piecewise expanding Markov maps of the interval, we construct Banach spaces adapted to the dynamics and obtain a complete description of the annealed resonance spectrum. Then we investigate an inverse spectral problem, proving realisability results for prescribed collections of complex numbers as resonances of suitably constructed annealed dynamical systems.
tldr: This paper extends Ruelle-Pollicott resonances to annealed random dynamical systems, providing spectral analysis and decorrelation formulas.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize the theory of Ruelle-Pollicott resonances, which describe decay of correlations in deterministic dynamical systems, to annealed random dynamical systems where maps are chosen i.i.d.
method: They introduce annealed transfer and Koopman operators, define resonances as point spectrum elements, and derive a decorrelation formula. They then construct Banach spaces for piecewise expanding Markov maps to fully describe the resonance spectrum and solve an inverse spectral problem.
result: They obtain a complete description of the annealed resonance spectrum for a family of piecewise expanding Markov maps and prove realisability results for prescribed resonance collections.
conclusion: The work establishes a framework for annealed Ruelle-Pollicott resonances, with explicit examples and inverse results, contributing to the theory of random dynamical systems.

title: Maximal Achievable Service Rates Of Some Classes Of Linear Codes
authors: Priyanka Choudhary, Monika Yadav, Maheshanand Bhaintwal
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate lower bounds on the maximum achievable service rates for data symbols in certain classes of linear codes, including cyclic codes and low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, that are derived from combinatorial structures such as [MATH]-designs, difference sets, and balanced incomplete block designs (BIBDs). We first establish a lower bound on the maximum achievable service rate for each data symbol in the following two cases: (i) systematic linear codes [MATH] under the assumption that the supports of codewords of a fixed weight in [MATH] form a BIBD, and (ii) non-systematic binary codes under the assumption that the supports of codewords of a fixed weight in [MATH] form a [MATH]-design. We then investigate the linear codes obtained from the incidence matrices of BIBDs, particularly certain classes of BIBD-LDPC codes, and show how the parameters of the underlying designs can be exploited to determine lower bounds on the maximum achievable service rates for the data symbols of the corresponding linear code. In addition, we analyze the maximum achievable service rates of systematic extended linear codes. We show that the existence of a symmetric BIBD (SBIBD) corresponding to a dual codeword can be used to derive a lower bound on the maximum achievable service rate of the associated systematic cyclic code. We also present some families of cyclic codes constructed from difference sets and obtain explicit lower bounds on the maximum achievable service rates for their data symbols. In particular, we determine the exact values of the maximum achievable service rates for each data symbol of cyclic codes arising from Singer difference sets.
tldr: This paper studies lower bounds on maximum achievable service rates for data symbols in certain linear codes (cyclic and LDPC) derived from combinatorial designs.
motivation: The paper aims to understand the service rates of linear codes, which is relevant to distributed storage and communication systems, but not directly to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
method: The authors use combinatorial structures such as BIBDs, difference sets, and designs to derive lower bounds on service rates for systematic and non-systematic codes, and analyze specific families like BIBD-LDPC codes and cyclic codes from Singer difference sets.
result: They establish lower bounds on maximum achievable service rates for various code classes and determine exact values for cyclic codes from Singer difference sets.
conclusion: The paper contributes to classical coding theory, but has no connection to quantum information or the other specified research directions.

title: A Damped Subspace Splitting Algorithm For Constrained Density Functional Theory
authors: Yuanming Su, Yukuan Hu, Xin Liu, Guanghui Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constrained density functional theory (CDFT) provides a powerful framework for describing electronically excited and charge-localized states, which underlie a broad range of physical and chemical phenomena. However, the discretized optimization problems arising from CDFT calculations remain challenging, owing to the presence of both the Stiefel manifold constraint and additional nonconvex quadratic constraints. Existing algorithms either fail to enforce the quadratic constraints with high accuracy or face convergence issues due to double-loop iterative structures. In this paper, we first derive a subspace-splitting reformulation that decouples the two groups of constraints, by exploiting the inherent rotation invariance and introducing a nonlinear subspace alignment constraint. Based on this reformulation, we propose a single-loop damped alternating direction method of multipliers, called DASSP. To the best of our knowledge, DASSP is the first algorithm for CDFT calculations with rigorous convergence guarantees. Each iteration of DASSP comprises a spectral minimization step, a projected gradient step, and a damped dual ascent step, all of which admit efficient implementations. Numerical results on synthetic and realistic CDFT problems demonstrate that DASSP attains high feasibility accuracy and exhibits favorable efficiency without compromising robustness. We expect that this work will pave the way toward reliable and efficient large-scale CDFT applications.
tldr: This paper proposes a new optimization algorithm for constrained density functional theory (CDFT) calculations, focusing on numerical efficiency and convergence guarantees.
motivation: CDFT is important for describing excited and charge-localized states, but existing algorithms struggle with constraint enforcement and convergence. The authors aim to develop a more reliable and efficient algorithm.
method: The authors derive a subspace-splitting reformulation that decouples Stiefel manifold and quadratic constraints, then propose a single-loop damped alternating direction method of multipliers (DASSP) with spectral minimization, projected gradient, and damped dual ascent steps.
result: Numerical experiments on synthetic and realistic CDFT problems show that DASSP achieves high feasibility accuracy and favorable efficiency without compromising robustness.
conclusion: DASSP is the first CDFT algorithm with rigorous convergence guarantees, potentially enabling large-scale CDFT applications.

title: Moment-based Linear Programming Bounds For Locally Recoverable Codes
authors: Shujian Li, Hengjia Wei, Maosheng Xiong
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we derive new Delsarte-type linear programming bounds for [MATH]-ary [MATH]-locally recoverable codes (LRCs) with three attributes: first, the variable set is comparable in size to that of the classical Delsarte LP; second, our LP exploits the higher-order information forced by the local-distance condition through order \(\delta-2\), in the sense that for nondegenerate linear codes, its balanced base part gives exactly the same dimension bound as the symmetrized refined-weight LP of Gruica, Jany, and Ravagnani, while the additional constraints, nonvacuous whenever [MATH], give a further strengthening; and third, it applies to general [MATH]-LRCs, linear and nonlinear alike. Extensive computations over binary and ternary alphabets show that the convex-hull LP yields improvements not captured by the previous LP and often sharpens the shortening and generalized Singleton bounds.
tldr: This paper derives new linear programming bounds for locally recoverable codes, a topic in classical coding theory with no quantum information or thermodynamics connection.
motivation: The paper aims to improve bounds for locally recoverable codes, which are important for distributed storage systems, but this is outside the user's research interests.
method: The authors develop Delsarte-type linear programming bounds that exploit higher-order information from the local-distance condition, and they compare with existing bounds.
result: The new LP bounds provide improvements over previous LP bounds and often sharpen the shortening and generalized Singleton bounds for binary and ternary alphabets.
conclusion: The paper contributes to classical coding theory but has no relevance to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Kernel Formula For Kinetic Fokker-Planck Equations
authors: Wuchen Li Fuqun Han
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive an explicit one-step kernel formula for the kinetic Fokker-Planck equation. The construction begins with a reference dynamics admitting an explicit transition kernel and uses a carefully chosen auxiliary weight to encode the drift perturbation. The resulting kernel formula provides an explicit approximation of the density evolution. In a weighted phase-space setting, we establish local weak consistency and first-order finite-time weak convergence under suitable regularity and moment assumptions. We also give a formal variational interpretation of the formula in terms of a regularized Wasserstein-type proximal operator and present analogous constructions for a broader class of parabolic equations. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy of the kernel approximation and its application to deterministic particle schemes for kinetic sampling.
tldr: This paper derives a kernel formula for kinetic Fokker-Planck equations, focusing on numerical approximation and particle schemes.
motivation: The authors aim to provide an explicit approximation for density evolution in kinetic Fokker-Planck equations, which are central to statistical physics and sampling.
method: They construct a reference dynamics with an explicit transition kernel and use an auxiliary weight to encode drift perturbation, establishing weak consistency and convergence.
result: The kernel formula provides an explicit approximation with first-order finite-time weak convergence under regularity assumptions, and numerical experiments show accuracy.
conclusion: The method offers a new numerical approach for kinetic Fokker-Planck equations, with potential applications in sampling and particle methods.

title: The Trust-Free Aggregation Layer Of The Unicity Infrastructure
authors: Risto Laanoja, Mike Gault, Dirk Draheim, Ahto Buldas
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unicity is a novel blockchain infrastructure for enabling users to execute off-chain peer-to-peer token transactions while preventing parallel states of tokens (double-spending) with minimal blockchain complexity and storage. A key component of the infrastructure is the Aggregation Layer responsible for storing information about the spent states of tokens and providing compact cryptographic proofs of no double-spending for the users without making any compromises in trust. Aggregation Layer is a layer 2 style service that holds an append-only key-value repository that periodically certifies its state using a traditional blockchain that we call the Consensus Layer. Every time while certifying a changed state the Aggregation Layer provides a cryptographic proof to the Consensus Layer about the append-only consistency of the key-value store. We use the Radix Sparse Merkle Trees (RSMTs) to create the cryptographic digest r_i of the store in every round i and authentication paths of special type in order to prove that the next digest r_{i+1} was obtained while only adding some key-value pairs (k,v) to the repository. The proof verification code is implemented as an Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR) circuit on top of the Plonky3 STARK toolkit. Our implementation uses no trusted setup, achieves throughput of 10,000 insertions per second and and millisecond range verification time on a single consumer-class CPU.
tldr: This paper presents a trust-free aggregation layer for a blockchain infrastructure using Radix Sparse Merkle Trees and STARK proofs to prevent double-spending.
motivation: The authors aim to enable off-chain token transactions with minimal blockchain complexity while preventing double-spending without compromising trust.
method: They design an append-only key-value store certified periodically by a consensus layer, using Radix Sparse Merkle Trees for cryptographic digests and authentication paths, with proof verification implemented as an AIR circuit on Plonky3 STARK.
result: The implementation achieves 10,000 insertions per second and millisecond-range verification on a consumer CPU, with no trusted setup.
conclusion: The aggregation layer provides an efficient and trust-free solution for double-spending prevention in blockchain systems.

title: Computationally Efficient Collaborative Communication Via Regularity-Based Coarsening
authors: Mark Bedaywi, Scott Emmons, Nika Haghtalab, Stuart Russell
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Our results show that the existence of a short high-utility protocol already suffices for efficient communication. In particular, in a game with [MATH] possible observations and [MATH] actions: (1) For any achievable target utility [MATH], we give an algorithm with [MATH] runtime that designs a protocol achieving utility at least [MATH] using only [MATH] bits of communication. Here, [MATH] is the minimum number of bits used by any protocol, even a computationally inefficient one, to achieve utility [MATH]. (2) We prove that this exponential dependence on [MATH] is tight up to a constant. That is, unless [MATH], no polynomial-time algorithm can in general find optimal protocols using fewer than [MATH] bits. We note that our results strictly weaken the assumptions required by prior work in the multi-agent information aggregation literature, filling a gap that had remained elusive even for games with constant [MATH]. In particular, prior guarantees for agreement-based information aggregation rely on structural assumptions such as informational substitutes or weak learnability. We show that these assumptions already imply [MATH] and are therefore more restrictive conditions than required by our protocol to succeed. On a technical level, our results involve a novel strengthening of the Frieze-Kannan weak regularity lemma and yield the following powerful polynomial-time transformation tool: for every communication game [MATH], it constructs a game [MATH] that is a coarsening of the agents' observation spaces into constant-size partitions, such that [MATH] and [MATH] are indistinguishable with respect to every short communication protocol. This coarsening theorem is the engine behind our algorithm and may be of independent interest.
tldr: This paper presents an algorithm for designing communication protocols in multi-agent games using a coarsening technique based on a strengthened weak regularity lemma, achieving near-optimal utility with exponentially fewer bits.
motivation: The authors aim to address the computational challenge of finding efficient communication protocols in multi-agent information aggregation, where prior work required restrictive structural assumptions.
method: They introduce a novel strengthening of the Frieze-Kannan weak regularity lemma to construct a coarsened game with constant-size observation partitions that is indistinguishable from the original game with respect to short protocols, enabling a polynomial-time algorithm.
result: The algorithm achieves utility at least the target with only O(2^m) bits, where m is the minimum bits needed by any protocol, and they prove this exponential dependence is tight unless P=NP.
conclusion: The results weaken assumptions for efficient communication and provide a general transformation tool that may be of independent interest.

title: Quantifying Bitcoin Network Resilience Through Critical Scenario Discovery: A Dual-Layer Framework For Discovering Contentious Fork Conditions In Decentralized Consensus
authors: Peter Foytik, Sachin Shetty, Ross Gore, Eranga Bandara
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bitcoin's consensus depends not only on protocol rules but on the emergent behavior of a heterogeneous network of nodes with divergent economic stakes. Whether a contentious soft fork resolves cleanly or fractures into a persistent chain split is difficult to predict analytically but can be explored through controlled experimentation. This paper applies Scenario Discovery, an ensemble-simulation methodology using the Patient Rule Induction Method (PRIM), to identify the configuration regions that produce contentious fork outcomes. Using Warnet to run real bitcoind nodes across 1,330 valid scenarios spanning economic weight, mining-pool commitment, pool ideology, hashrate, and difficulty-retarget regime, we identify the parameter thresholds separating clean resolution from contested split. We show that economic weight distribution across a partition, not hashrate majority, is the primary determinant of resolution under Bitcoin's operational retarget interval and moderate price divergence. Three findings follow: an economic-support floor (0.45-0.50) and override ceiling (0.78-0.82) bound the contested space, with an Economic Self-Sustaining Point (0.74) between them; a pool-commitment "flip-point" (0.214 of committed hashrate) at which committing the largest pool to the upgrading chain paradoxically reverses the outcome; and outcomes resolve on two independent layers, hashrate and economic adoption, governed by different parameters. Individual user nodes show no detectable influence on fork outcomes under the modeled economic weightings. We close with three monitoring questions, answerable from public data, that translate these thresholds into operational guidance.
tldr: This paper uses scenario discovery and PRIM to identify conditions leading to contentious Bitcoin forks, focusing on economic and hashrate dynamics.
motivation: Predicting whether a contentious soft fork will cause a chain split is difficult analytically; the authors aim to find parameter thresholds that lead to such splits.
method: They run 1,330 simulations using Warnet with real bitcoind nodes, varying economic weight, mining-pool commitment, pool ideology, hashrate, and difficulty-retarget regime, then apply PRIM to identify regions of contentious outcomes.
result: Economic weight distribution, not hashrate majority, primarily determines fork resolution; they find an economic-support floor (0.45-0.50), override ceiling (0.78-0.82), and a pool-commitment flip-point (0.214).
conclusion: The study provides operational thresholds and monitoring questions for predicting fork outcomes, but it is not directly related to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: AI-Farol: Co-Evolutionary Dynamics In A Multi-Agent Two-Sided Learning Framework
authors: Iosif Polenakis, Kalliopi Kastampolidou, Theodore Andronikos
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The El Farol Bar game is a classical model of coordination under uncertainty that traditionally treats the venue as a passive constraint. In this work, we reconceptualize the problem by modeling the bar as a strategic player endowed with AI-driven learning capabilities. We extend the original framework in two principal directions: first, by introducing partial observability, whereby agents observe only subsets of past attendees; and second, by transforming the bar from a passive capacity threshold into an active mechanism designer that adjusts pricing policies to balance revenue, utilization, and sustainability constraints. Agents employ AI-based learning to form beliefs and adapt attendance strategies under incomplete information, while the bar applies policy learning to optimize dynamic pricing. The resulting two-sided learning system frames coordination as a co-evolutionary process between boundedly rational agents and an adaptive institution, offering insights into congestion management, resource allocation, and mechanism design in complex adaptive systems.
tldr: This paper extends the El Farol Bar game into a two-sided learning framework where both agents and the bar adapt, but it is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to model coordination under uncertainty with an adaptive institution, but the context is classical multi-agent systems and mechanism design.
method: They introduce partial observability and AI-based learning for agents, and policy learning for the bar to adjust pricing, forming a co-evolutionary system.
result: The paper provides insights into congestion management and resource allocation in complex adaptive systems, but no quantum or thermodynamic content.
conclusion: The work is purely classical and does not connect to any of the four research directions.

title: Enhancing Anomaly Resilience In Research Networks: A Large-Scale Forecasting Benchmark For Dynamic Security Baselining
authors: Byrav Ramamurthy Mohammad Arafath Uddin Shariff
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Research and Education Networks (RENs) serve as critical infrastructure for scientific discovery, yet they face a unique security paradox: their normal traffic patterns which are characterized by massive, bursty "elephant flows" are statistically indistinguishable from volumetric attacks such as DDoS to conventional monitoring systems. This similarity leads to high false-positive rates in anomaly detection, blinding security operators to genuine threats. In this paper, we propose and evaluate a high-fidelity traffic forecasting framework designed to establish dynamic security baselines for RENs. Leveraging an exclusive 57-day Internet2 dataset spanning ten backbone routers (13.7 billion packets), we perform the first large-scale benchmark of anomaly-aware forecasting models in this domain. We systematically evaluate six model families, from SARIMA to state-of-the-art long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST), across 960 experimental configurations. Our results demonstrate that these advanced architectures, particularly TiDE, reduce baseline prediction error by 30-42% compared to traditional methods ([MATH]), significantly improving the distinction between legitimate scientific bursts and potential anomalies. Furthermore, we introduce a novel anomaly-integration strategy that improves model robustness by 3.3% in the presence of noise. This work provides the first statistically validated framework for distinguishing scientific workflows from network attacks, enabling more autonomous and resilient network security operations.
tldr: This paper benchmarks traffic forecasting models for anomaly detection in research networks, which is unrelated to quantum information science.
motivation: Research and Education Networks face security challenges due to traffic patterns resembling attacks; the authors aim to improve anomaly detection via dynamic baselines.
method: Using a 57-day Internet2 dataset, they evaluate six forecasting model families (SARIMA to TiDE, PatchTST) across 960 configurations, and introduce an anomaly-integration strategy.
result: Advanced architectures, especially TiDE, reduce prediction error by 30-42% and improve robustness by 3.3% in noisy conditions.
conclusion: The framework provides statistically validated baselines to distinguish scientific traffic from attacks, enhancing network security operations.

title: LC-Implicit-QAOA: Active-Workspace-Capped Exact Objective-and-Gradient Evaluation For Training Over Bounded Qubo Light Cones
authors: Chih-Chung Hsu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: QAOA training repeatedly queries an objective and all shared gradients, making exact evaluation a feasibility bottleneck even when QUBO terms have bounded causal cones. Building on established causal-cone restriction and adjoint differentiation, LC-Implicit-QAOA profiles cone structure and induced-edge counts before local-amplitude and named-workspace allocation, then jointly selects equal-size microbatches and checkpoint schedules under a named active-evaluator workspace budget. "Implicit" means omitting both global state and global cost table, not implicit differentiation; infeasible requests are rejected before those allocations. An independently implemented complex128/float64 dense adjoint agrees with LC over 1,800 graph-angle comparisons, with a worst relative gradient error of 1.56 x 10^-13. LC completes all 104 target requests in a p=2 bounded-cone grid; under a prespecified n <= 24 validation cap, the matched state-plus-cost reference is executed for 28 requests and deliberately not run on 76. Across 80 budgeted requests, measured allocated evaluator memory stays within budget, reaching at most 0.797 of it. On 3-regular n=512, p=2, the adjoint reaches the same finite-budget endpoint in 101 objective-equivalent calls and 189 s, versus 909 calls and 1,565 s for central differences. LC targets fixed-depth one- and two-local diagonal QUBO costs with a transverse-field mixer; it provides neither global states, sampling, nor a hardware-independent fastest-backend rule.
tldr: This paper presents an optimization technique for QAOA training that uses causal-cone restriction and adjoint differentiation to efficiently evaluate objectives and gradients under a workspace budget.
motivation: QAOA training is bottlenecked by repeated exact objective and gradient evaluations, even when QUBO terms have bounded causal cones. The authors aim to improve efficiency by exploiting the structure of these cones.
method: The method profiles cone structure and induced-edge counts, then jointly selects microbatches and checkpoint schedules under a named active-evaluator workspace budget. It omits global state and cost tables, and uses dense adjoint differentiation for gradient computation.
result: The method matches a reference implementation with high precision, completes all target requests within budget, and reduces computational cost significantly compared to central differences on a 3-regular graph with n=512.
conclusion: The proposed LC-Implicit-QAOA provides an efficient exact evaluation strategy for QAOA training, but it is a specialized optimization technique without direct connection to the user's research interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Rasp-qaoa: Resource-Aware Per-Instance Selection For Exact Qaoa Simulation
authors: Chih-Chung Hsu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact QAOA simulation spans several computational representations whose useful regions differ sharply across graph structure, circuit depth, precision, and available memory. Choosing only a backend name hides these differences: an executable choice also fixes the representation, adapter, precision mode, and memory policy. We introduce RASP-QAOA, a per-instance selector over ten such actions. It first removes actions that cannot implement the requested QAOA semantics or execution requirements, then orders the remaining actions using instance features; actions outside learned support are handled by analytical work estimates. On a content-disjoint 60-request H200 evaluation, RASP-QAOA succeeds on all 31 requests for which at least one admissible action completes and validates. Within this set it reaches 27/31 top-1 and 31/31 top-2 selection, with 1.051 geometric-mean regret. Its failure-penalized PAR10 score is 0.0396 times that of development-selected CUAOA (95% interval: 0.0085-0.1644). A separate 30-request crossover shows that graph structure changes 16 decisions and improves the paired penalized score, while a depth-1 stump matches gradient boosting. The evidence supports resource-aware representation selection at n <= 35, p <= 5, with gains driven by representation features rather than classifier complexity.
tldr: This paper introduces RASP-QAOA, a per-instance selector for choosing among ten computational representations for exact QAOA simulation, focusing on resource-aware selection.
motivation: Exact QAOA simulation performance varies significantly across representations depending on graph structure, circuit depth, precision, and memory, and choosing only a backend name hides these differences.
method: RASP-QAOA filters out inadmissible actions, then ranks remaining actions using instance features, with analytical work estimates for out-of-support cases.
result: On a 60-request evaluation, RASP-QAOA achieves 27/31 top-1 and 31/31 top-2 selection with low regret, and outperforms a baseline in failure-penalized score.
conclusion: The results support resource-aware representation selection for QAOA simulation, with gains driven by representation features rather than classifier complexity.

title: On The Figures Of Merit For Quantum Software Security: Toward A Benchmarking Rubric
authors: Badhon Rahman, Majid Haghparast, Tommi Mikkonen
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum software is increasingly provided through multi-tenant and cloud-based Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) stacks. A growing concern about the diverse attack vectors across the pipeline has been demonstrated in recent research. Yet the community has converged on three mature pillars: Scale (Qubit Count), Quality (Quantum Volume), and Speed (Circuit Layer Operations per Second (CLOPS)) for the merit performance figures. Moreover, it has also begun to define software-quality metrics. However, the security of quantum software remains largely unmeasured. A few quantitative security indicators, such as Total Variation Distance (TVD) and Degree of Functional Corruption (DFC), exist. Although they were introduced ad hoc for individual circuit obfuscation techniques, they are incompatible. We assert that the security of quantum software deserves the same attention as the performance: an explicit set of Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs). The research of this paper is threefold: (i) characterizes a three-layer measurement gap, (ii) proposes a structured S-FoM set organized by ISO/IEC 25010 security sub-characteristics, QaaS pipeline mapping, and measurement maturity, and (iii) defines a benchmarking rubric that normalizes and aggregates S-FoMs into a combined Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score. Additionally, an illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques has been presented. Our aim is a first step toward security-aware benchmarking of the Quantum Software Stack (QSS).
tldr: This paper proposes a benchmarking rubric for quantum software security, focusing on security figures of merit rather than quantum information theory or physics.
motivation: Quantum software security is largely unmeasured, and existing metrics are ad hoc and incompatible, so the authors aim to establish a structured set of security figures of merit.
method: The authors characterize a three-layer measurement gap, propose a structured S-FoM set based on ISO/IEC 25010, and define a rubric that aggregates S-FoMs into a Quantum Software Security Posture score.
result: They present an illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques to demonstrate the rubric's application.
conclusion: The work is a first step toward security-aware benchmarking of the quantum software stack, but it is not directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: An End-to-End Threat Model For The Quantum-as-a-Service Pipeline
authors: Badhon Rahman, Majid Haghparast, Tommi Mikkonen
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud-based accessing of Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) platforms such as IBM Quantum, IonQ Cloud, and Amazon Braket is becoming popular day by day. Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (VQE, QAOA, QML) transfer data via a long layered pipeline of orchestration, compilation, and execution. Recent works have demonstrated various critical attacks at individual stages: Calibration tampering, SWAP attacks, QubitHammer, and so on. However, these attacks remain separated because of their own terminology, and existing STRIDE-based threat modeling in the context of quantum lacks a structured view towards the QaaS stack itself. We address this concern by decomposing the workflow into six-stage model with STRIDE threat modeling. Our matrix demonstrated attack vectors in quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible tiers for each of the stages. We further investigate the underexplored sections (repudiation and elevation-of-privilege) and distinguish three different cross-stage attack chains with higher impacts.
tldr: This paper proposes a STRIDE-based threat model for the Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) pipeline, decomposing the workflow into six stages and analyzing attack vectors.
motivation: Existing security analyses of QaaS platforms are fragmented, lacking a structured view of the entire pipeline. The authors aim to provide a comprehensive threat model to identify and categorize vulnerabilities.
method: The authors decompose the QaaS workflow into six stages and apply STRIDE threat modeling to each, creating a matrix of attack vectors. They also investigate underexplored threat categories and identify cross-stage attack chains.
result: The paper presents a structured threat model with a matrix of attack vectors across stages, highlighting quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible threats. It also identifies three cross-stage attack chains with higher impact.
conclusion: The proposed threat model provides a systematic framework for understanding and mitigating security risks in QaaS pipelines, though it is not directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
