title: Ion Coulomb Crystals: An Exotic Form Of Condensed Matter
authors: Giovanna Morigi, John Bollinger, Michael Drewsen, Daniel Podolsky, And Efrat Shimshoni
abstract:
Author(s): Giovanna Morigi, John Bollinger, Michael Drewsen, Daniel Podolsky, and Efrat Shimshoni

Coulomb crystals form when the Coulomb interaction between charged particles dominates over kinetic energy; the prototype is the Wigner crystal formed by conduction electrons in metals at low densities. In recent years, it has become possible to realize Coulomb crystals using laser-cooled trapped ions, and these systems allow for unprecedented control of experimental parameters. This review describes the state of the art of ion Coulomb crystals in one, two, and three dimensions, their properties in and out of equilibrium, and their importance across fields ranging from condensed matter to astrophysics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 035001] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: A review of ion Coulomb crystals as a platform for studying condensed matter phenomena, with emphasis on their equilibrium and non-equilibrium properties.

method: The paper reviews experimental and theoretical work on ion Coulomb crystals in 1D, 2D, and 3D, covering structural phases, dynamics, and applications.
result: It summarizes the state of the art, highlighting the versatility of ion crystals for simulating condensed matter models and studying phase transitions.
conclusion: Ion Coulomb crystals are a valuable tool for fundamental physics, but the review does not directly advance the user's specific research directions.

Active matter has become a lively topic in recent years, but what exactly is meant by the term ‘active matter’ is often unclear. This Colloquium discusses the scientific and semantic issues underlying this ambiguity, as well as the history of the field, and offers a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems. It then surveys recent developments including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review covers tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution, a technique in nanoscale optical imaging.
motivation: To provide an overview of tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy, which combines scanning probe techniques with optical fluorescence to achieve superresolution at the atomic scale, enabling study of molecular electronic and vibronic properties.
method: The paper is a review that discusses the principles, techniques, and applications of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy, including the use of a scanning tip as a nanoscale optical antenna.
result: The review highlights that this technique achieves atomic-scale spatial resolution, overcoming the diffraction limit, and provides new insights into molecular structures and reactions.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy is a powerful tool for nanoscale imaging and spectroscopy, with potential for further developments in molecular identification and characterization.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications, including magnetism, topology, and dynamics.
motivation: To summarize the rapidly evolving field of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials, which has revealed new phenomena and challenges established theories.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes current knowledge on 2D magnets, discussing experimental and theoretical advances across various subfields.
result: The review highlights the breadth of the field, including ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, and interactions with light and electric fields.
conclusion: The field of 2D van der Waals magnets is actively expanding, offering new fundamental insights and potential applications.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, discussing electronic structure, correlation effects, and observed phenomena.
result: It highlights the emergence of topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, and various correlated states, and discusses their implications.
conclusion: Kagome metals serve as a platform for exploring strongly correlated topological physics, but the paper does not directly contribute to the specified research directions.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, unifying approaches for chemical, ecological, and epidemiological models.
motivation: To provide a unified framework for modeling complex systems with many interacting agents using field-theoretic techniques.
method: The review synthesizes various field-theoretic methods (e.g., path integrals, Doi-Peliti) applied to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.
result: Presents a comprehensive overview of how these methods can be applied across disciplines, highlighting their versatility.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods offer a powerful and unifying approach to study stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, with broad applicability.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of how neutron star observations constrain the dense matter equation of state.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities, which is relevant to nuclear physics and astrophysics.
method: Reviews gravitational-wave and X-ray observations of neutron stars and compares them to theoretical predictions from nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Summarizes current constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities.
conclusion: Neutron star observations provide valuable constraints on the equation of state, with future observations expected to improve them.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with broad applications to physical systems.
motivation: To update the field of spin glasses and highlight the synergy between experimental, theoretical, and computational approaches.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes progress in spin-glass research, including experimental findings, theoretical models, and large-scale simulations.
result: The review tracks the evolution of the field and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass research benefits from interdisciplinary collaboration, and the review provides a comprehensive overview for researchers.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are exotic states of matter with potential applications in quantum computing, but their realization in materials is challenging.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (Kitaev model) and experimental progress in candidate materials, highlighting chiral edge modes and other topological features.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of Kitaev spin liquids and identifies promising materials for further study.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids are a rich field with potential for topological quantum computation, but more work is needed to confirm and control these states.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review connects statistical physics methods (maximum entropy, renormalization group) to large-scale neural recordings, but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The paper aims to bridge statistical physics and neuroscience to understand collective neural activity, but this is outside the user's research interests.
method: It reviews applications of maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to multi-neuron recording data.
result: It highlights reproducible behaviors in neural networks and argues for predictive power of statistical physics principles in neuroscience.
conclusion: The paper concludes that statistical physics can provide quantitative insights into brain function, but it is not relevant to the user's quantum-focused research directions.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical approaches to internal conversion, a fundamental photophysical process, and to highlight their relevance to applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper is a review that surveys various theoretical models and methods used to describe internal conversion, discussing their strengths and limitations.
result: The review synthesizes existing knowledge on internal conversion and outlines how these methods can be incorporated into applied studies.
conclusion: The authors conclude that theoretical methods for internal conversion are mature and can be applied to practical problems, but the paper does not present new research findings.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum-mechanical aspects of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their formation and quantum features.
motivation: To provide an overview of quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential applications in spintronics and quantum technologies.
method: The paper is a review article that synthesizes theoretical and experimental results on skyrmion physics, including quantum interactions and quantum effects.
result: It discusses the quantum-mechanical origins of skyrmion stability and dynamics, and explores potential quantum functionalities such as quantum computing and sensing.
conclusion: Magnetic skyrmions exhibit rich quantum phenomena that could be harnessed for future technologies, but the field is still developing.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the Standard Model, potentially mediated by new bosons and related to dark matter.
motivation: To summarize the state of the art in searches for new spin-dependent forces, which could reveal physics beyond the Standard Model and shed light on dark matter and dark energy.
method: The paper is a review, synthesizing theoretical frameworks for exotic spin-dependent interactions and experimental techniques used to probe them, including precision measurements and atomic/molecular spectroscopy.
result: The review catalogs numerous theoretical models and experimental constraints, highlighting the current limits on coupling constants and the potential for future discoveries.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, with many experimental efforts ongoing and future improvements expected.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining that apparent violations arise from violating assumptions in the bounds' derivations.
motivation: To clarify why some measured material properties exceed classical thermodynamic bounds and to show how designing materials to violate these assumptions can yield interesting properties.
method: A review of various circumstances where measurements exceed thermodynamic bounds, analyzing which underlying assumptions are violated in each case.
result: Identifies multiple classes of materials and measurement conditions that lead to apparent violations, and discusses how to exploit these for material design.
conclusion: Apparent violations of thermodynamic bounds are due to assumption violations, and understanding this can guide development of materials with exceptional properties.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical implementations of synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries such as fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions.
motivation: To explore exotic geometries that enable simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: The paper surveys various platforms (atomic, photonic, electronic) and theoretical approaches for realizing these geometries.
result: It provides an overview of current progress and challenges in simulating quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries.
conclusion: The field is promising for simulating novel physics, but it is not directly aligned with the user's specific research directions.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: This review explores self-alignment in active matter systems, where particles align their orientation with their velocity, leading to novel collective behaviors.
motivation: To unify and understand the role of self-alignment in active matter, which is a key mechanism in biological and robotic systems.
method: The paper provides a comprehensive review, introducing a unified mathematical framework and surveying existing models and experiments.
result: It highlights how self-alignment leads to phenomena such as orbiting in traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, and discusses potential applications.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a fundamental principle in active matter with broad implications for biology, materials science, and robotics.

title: Excitons In 2H-MoTe2: Anisotropies, Masses And Binding Energy
authors: Zahra Ahmadi Heidari And Martin Knupfer
abstract: Bound electron–hole pairs called excitons determine the photophysical behavior of semiconducting materials. In this study, we present a combination of electron energy-loss spectroscopy in transmission and optical absorption spectroscopy for the investigation of excitons in bulk 2H-MoTe2. The exciton dispersion E(q) was measured for momentum transfers oriented along the ΓK and ΓM directions at 20 K. From the extracted dispersion relations, the in-plane exciton effective mass was determined. Our results reveal that for 2H-MoTe2 the exciton effective mass is anisotropic. In consideration of the complementary optical results the exciton reduced mass, binding energy and radius have been determined.
tldr: This paper studies exciton properties in bulk 2H-MoTe2 using electron energy-loss spectroscopy and optical absorption, focusing on anisotropic effective masses and binding energy.
motivation: Understanding exciton behavior in transition metal dichalcogenides is important for optoelectronic applications, but this work is primarily a materials characterization study.
method: The authors combine electron energy-loss spectroscopy in transmission and optical absorption spectroscopy to measure exciton dispersion along ΓK and ΓM directions at 20 K, extracting effective masses and binding parameters.
result: They find anisotropic in-plane exciton effective mass and determine reduced mass, binding energy, and radius.
conclusion: The study provides detailed exciton parameters for 2H-MoTe2, but it does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Low-dimensional Dynamical Behavior Of Locally Coupled Chiral Swarmalators
authors: Zihan Li, Yonggang Wu, Xiaoyu Zhang, Zhigang Zheng And Duxin Chen
abstract: Understanding the dynamical behavior of swarmalators, particularly the transition from disorder to synchronization, constitutes one of the pivotal frontiers in the study of complex systems. We propose an ansatz that successfully decouples the spatial and phase dynamics in the locally coupled chiral swarmalators model, enabling rigorous analytical treatment of this complex system. Within this framework, we systematically examine how the interaction radius affects system synchronization, quantified through an order parameter measuring phase coherence. Our theoretical analysis reveals that increasing the interaction radius enhances synchronization in both velocity and phase dynamics. This relationship demonstrates that larger interaction networks facilitate more efficient information transfer among heterogeneous oscillators with different intrinsic frequencies. Using a self-consistent approach in the thermodynamic limit, we derive analytical expressions for the order parameter that accurately predict the synchronization transition. These findings provide fundamental insights into synchronization mechanisms in spatially embedded swarmalator systems with applications in understanding biological collective behaviors.
tldr: This paper analyzes synchronization in a model of chiral swarmalators with local coupling, deriving analytical expressions for the order parameter.
motivation: To understand the transition from disorder to synchronization in spatially embedded oscillator systems, which is relevant to biological collective behaviors.
method: The authors propose an ansatz to decouple spatial and phase dynamics, then use a self-consistent approach in the thermodynamic limit to derive analytical expressions for the order parameter.
result: They find that increasing the interaction radius enhances synchronization in both velocity and phase dynamics, and their analytical predictions match the synchronization transition.
conclusion: The work provides insights into synchronization mechanisms in swarmalator systems, but it is not directly related to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Generalized K -space Coherent Averaging Method For Engineering Lattices Of Spin–orbit B...
authors: Pinki Chahal, Naume Shentevski, Priyanka Vadnere, David G Cory, Owen Lailey, Dmitry A Pushin And Dusan Sarenac
abstract: Spin–orbit beams, in which the orbital angular momentum degree of freedom is coupled to a two-level system such as polarization of light or spin in electrons and neutrons, have gained significant interest for their unique propagation properties and potential applications in imaging, material characterization, optical trapping, and quantum information processing. In this work we introduce a method for generating and engineering two-dimensional lattices of such spin–orbit beams based on coherent averaging in -space. By programming the angle, amplitude, and polarization of a set of input beams we obtain precise control over lattice geometry and period, as well as the orbital and radial degrees of freedom inside each unit cell. We explore both electromagnetic and matter wave implementations, and we experimentally demonstrate the generation and characterization of a micron-scale optical hexagonal lattice with well defined orbital and radial numbers in each unit cell. The described methods provide a robust and general method of generating and controlling structured waves such as optical skyrmions and matter wave implementations of orbit and spin–orbit beams.
tldr: This paper introduces a generalized k-space coherent averaging method for generating two-dimensional lattices of spin-orbit beams, with experimental demonstration in optics.
motivation: To provide a robust and general method for engineering structured waves such as optical skyrmions and matter-wave implementations of spin-orbit beams, which have potential applications in imaging, material characterization, and quantum information processing.
method: The method programs the angle, amplitude, and polarization of input beams to control lattice geometry, period, and orbital/radial degrees of freedom within each unit cell, using coherent averaging in k-space. Both electromagnetic and matter-wave implementations are explored.
result: Experimental demonstration of a micron-scale optical hexagonal lattice with well-defined orbital and radial numbers in each unit cell.
conclusion: The method provides a robust and general approach for generating and controlling structured waves, with potential applications in quantum information processing and other fields.

title: A Study Of The Dimer-trimer Crossover In A Driven Three-component Fermi Gas
authors: R Slowinski, G Servignat, F Chevy And C Lobo
abstract: We develop an effective field theory for a system with three distinguishable atomic species and present a variational calculation of the two and three-body binding energies in vacuum and in the presence of a single Fermi sea. Specifically, we consider the case where the interaction between first two atomic species is externally driven so as to produce a (non-universal) closed-channel dimer whose coupling can be controlled independently of all other interactions. We then model the remaining interactions as a contact interaction between the dimer and a third atomic species which forms the medium. We derive analytical expressions for the dimer and trimer binding energies in vacuum and in medium, and in the latter case we predict a crossing between the dimer and trimer branches as a function of the atom–dimer scattering length, analogous to the usual polaron and molecule problem. Furthermore, we show that the position of this crossing can be controlled by varying the atom–atom coupling that results from the external drive and we discuss the implications of these findings.
tldr: This paper develops an effective field theory for a driven three-component Fermi gas, studying dimer-trimer crossover in vacuum and in a Fermi sea.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the crossover between dimer and trimer states in a driven three-component Fermi gas, which is relevant to ultracold atomic physics.
method: They use an effective field theory with a variational calculation to compute two- and three-body binding energies in vacuum and in the presence of a Fermi sea, modeling the dimer as a closed channel with tunable coupling.
result: They derive analytical expressions for dimer and trimer binding energies and predict a crossing between the dimer and trimer branches as a function of atom-dimer scattering length, controllable by the external drive.
conclusion: The findings have implications for controlling few-body states in driven Fermi gases, but the topic is not aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Converting P T -symmetric Topological Classes By Floquet En...
authors: Ming-Jian Gao And Jun-Hong An
abstract: Going beyond the conventional classification rule of Altland-Zirnbauer symmetry classes, symmetric topological phases are classified by or . The interconversion between the two -symmetric topological classes is generally difficult due to the constraint of . Here, we propose a scheme to control and interconvert the -symmetric topological classes by Floquet engineering. We find that it is the removal of the gauge degree of freedom, induced by the phase difference between different hopping rates, by the periodic driving that leads to such an interconversion. Relaxing the system from the constraint of , rich exotic topological phases, e.g. the coexisting -symmetric first-order real Chern insulator and second-order topological insulator not only in different quasienergy gaps, but also in one single gap, are generated. In contrast to conventional Floquet topological phases, our result provides a way to realize exotic topological phases without changing symmetries. It enriches the family of topological phases and gives an insightful guidance for the development of multifunctional quantum devices.
tldr: This paper proposes Floquet engineering to interconvert PT-symmetric topological classes, generating exotic topological phases without changing symmetries.
motivation: The interconversion between PT-symmetric topological classes is difficult due to symmetry constraints, and the authors aim to control this via periodic driving.
method: They use Floquet engineering to remove gauge degrees of freedom induced by phase differences in hopping rates, enabling topological class interconversion.
result: They demonstrate coexisting PT-symmetric first-order real Chern insulator and second-order topological insulator in different quasienergy gaps and even in a single gap.
conclusion: The work enriches topological phases and provides guidance for multifunctional quantum devices, but it is not aligned with the user's research directions.

title: Probing Quark Electromagnetic Properties Via Entangled Quark Pairs In Fragmentation Hadrons At Lepton Colliders
authors: Qing-Hong Cao, Guanghui Li, Xin-Kai Wen And Bin Yan
abstract: Electromagnetic dipole interactions of light quarks induce distinct spin correlations in quark pairs produced at lepton colliders, favoring entangled spin-triplet state aligned along the axis or spin-singlet state. These correlations lead to unique azimuthal asymmetries in inclusive -dihadron pair production and in back-to-back hadron pairs ( ), which are absent in the SM. Using published Belle and BaBar measurements together with projected sensitivities based on ratios of azimuthal asymmetries, we demonstrate that these measurements provide significant constraints on light-quark dipole couplings, with a reduced dependence on poorly known nonperturbative fragmentation functions and free from contamination by other new physics effects. This approach offers a clean and novel probe of light-quark dipole interactions in collider experiments.
tldr: This paper proposes using spin correlations in entangled quark pairs from lepton colliders to probe light-quark electromagnetic dipole moments, with constraints from Belle and BaBar data.
motivation: The study aims to provide a clean probe of light-quark dipole interactions, which are poorly constrained and could reveal new physics beyond the Standard Model.
method: The authors analyze azimuthal asymmetries in dihadron production from entangled quark pairs, using published Belle and BaBar measurements and projected sensitivities to constrain dipole couplings.
result: They demonstrate that these measurements can significantly constrain light-quark dipole couplings with reduced dependence on fragmentation functions and minimal contamination from other new physics.
conclusion: This approach offers a novel and clean method to probe light-quark dipole interactions in collider experiments.

title: El Agente Cuántico: Automating Quantum Simulations
authors: Ignacio Gustin, Luis Mantilla Calderón, Juan B Pérez-Sánchez, Chris Crebolder, Jérôme F Gonthier, Mohammad Ghazi Vakili, Yuma Nakamura, Karthik Panicker, Manav Ramprasad, Aiwei Yin, Zijian Zhang, Yunheng Zou, Varinia Bernales And Alán Aspuru-Guzik
abstract: Quantum simulation is central to understanding and designing quantum systems across physics and chemistry. However, its practical use is often limited by the exponential growth of Hilbert space and by the increasing complexity of modern quantum-simulation software. Here we introduce El Agente Cuántico, a multi-agent AI system that automates quantum-simulation workflows by translating natural-language scientific intent into executed and validated computations across heterogeneous quantum-software frameworks. By reasoning directly over library documentation and APIs, our agentic system dynamically assembles end-to-end simulations spanning—but not limited to—state preparation, closed- and open-system dynamics, tensor-network methods, quantum control, quantum error correction, and quantum resource estimation. The developed system unifies traditionally distinct simulation paradigms behind a single natural-language interface. Beyond reducing technical barriers, this approach opens a path toward scalable, adaptive, and increasingly autonomous quantum simulation, enabling faster exploration of physical models, rapid hypothesis testing, and closer integration between theory, simulation, and emerging quantum hardware.
tldr: This paper introduces an AI agent system for automating quantum simulations via natural language, but it does not align with the specified research directions.
motivation: Quantum simulation is limited by complexity and software heterogeneity; the authors aim to lower barriers and automate workflows.
method: They develop a multi-agent AI system that translates natural-language scientific intent into executed and validated computations across various quantum-software frameworks.
result: The system unifies different simulation paradigms behind a single interface, enabling end-to-end simulations including state preparation, dynamics, tensor networks, control, error correction, and resource estimation.
conclusion: This approach reduces technical barriers and paves the way for more autonomous quantum simulation, but it is not a core contribution to the user's research interests.

title: From Intuition To Optimization: A Review Of Inverse Design Applied To Optical Nanotweezers
authors: Sejeong Kim And Kenneth B Crozier Damian Nelson
abstract: Optical nanotweezers, which integrate nanophotonic structures such as plasmonic antennas, dielectric resonators, and metasurfaces, have emerged as powerful tools for manipulating nanoparticles, biomolecules, and viruses with high precision. However, traditional designs rely heavily on heuristic approaches and simple geometries, limiting performance. Inverse design offers a paradigm shift by using computational optimization methods to discover non-intuitive, high-performance structures for optical trapping. This review provides an overview of key inverse design methodologies, including adjoint-based optimization, topology optimization, and machine learning approaches, and highlights their broader impact across nanophotonics. We then focus on their application to optical nanotweezers, where recent advances demonstrate enhanced trapping stiffness, reduced optical heating, and tailored trapping landscapes. Representative examples include algorithmic design of plasmonic nanotweezers, topology-optimized plasmonic nanoapertures, inverse-designed dielectric nanocavities, and force-centric designs based on Maxwell stress tensor engineering. Collectively, these studies illustrate how inverse design enables stable, efficient, and versatile optical trapping at the nanoscale. Despite these advances, challenges remain in fabrication, computational cost, and the interpretability of optimized structures. We conclude with a perspective on future directions, emphasizing opportunities in reconfigurable tweezers, lab-on-a-chip integration, and quantum nanophotonics. By bridging photonic optimization with nanoscale manipulation, inverse-designed optical nanotweezers offer promising opportunities for future applications in biophysics, materials science, and quantum technologies.
tldr: A review of inverse design methods applied to optical nanotweezers, focusing on computational optimization for nanophotonic trapping structures.
motivation: Traditional optical nanotweezer designs rely on heuristics and simple geometries, limiting performance; inverse design offers a computational approach to discover optimized structures.
method: The paper reviews inverse design methodologies including adjoint-based optimization, topology optimization, and machine learning, and surveys their applications to optical nanotweezers.
result: Recent advances demonstrate enhanced trapping stiffness, reduced heating, and tailored trapping landscapes, with examples of plasmonic and dielectric designs.
conclusion: Inverse design enables stable and efficient optical trapping, but challenges remain in fabrication, computational cost, and interpretability; future directions include reconfigurable tweezers and quantum nanophotonics.

title: Review On Band Structure And Spin Polarization Of Altermagnetic Materials
authors: Xiangnan Xie, Xiaoyue He, Fayuan Zhang And Chaoyu Chen
abstract: Recent theoretical and experimental efforts have revealed the existence of a new class of magnetic materials, altermagnets, characterized by distinct symmetries in spin and real space. Combining the properties of ferromagnets, such as band spin polarization and time-reversal symmetry breaking responses, and antiferromagnets, like vanishing stray field and terahertz magnon dynamics, altermagnets are attracting enormous attention in both magnetism and spintronics community. While numerous altermagnetic candidates and emerging physical properties have been studied in theory extensively and enthusiastically, the experimental investigation of altermagnetism is struggling against the lack of proper altermagnetic materials and the controversial results reported for specific candidates. In this review, we first give a general description on the concept and key properties of altermagnetism, outline its distinction from other compensated magnetic order from the aspects of time-reversal symmetry in the spin momentum locking texture and time-reversal symmetry breaking responses. The main body of this review concentrates on the progress in altermagnetic material study with special focus on their band structure and spin polarization features, as well as the controversies over several candidate materials. Going forward, we point out several directions which altermagnetic material investigation might follow and guidelines which could help to avoid the pitfalls in the experimental pursuit of ideal altermagnets.
tldr: A review of altermagnetic materials focusing on their band structure and spin polarization, highlighting experimental challenges.
motivation: To consolidate the theoretical and experimental progress on altermagnets, a new class of magnetic materials with potential spintronic applications, and to address controversies in candidate materials.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes recent theoretical and experimental findings on altermagnetism, comparing it with ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, and discussing band structure and spin polarization features.
result: The review outlines key properties of altermagnets, summarizes candidate materials and their band structures, and identifies experimental pitfalls and future research directions.
conclusion: Altermagnetic materials are promising for spintronics, but experimental verification is challenging; more suitable materials and careful characterization are needed.

title: Switchable Band Alignment In 2D-perovskite/WS2 Heterostructures For Tunable Exciton Transport And Valley Polarization
authors: Yingying Chen, Zeyi Liu, Zisheng Gong, Cheng Wang, Wendian Yao, Junze Li, Ti Wang, Weibo Gao And Dehui Li
abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures integrated by two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) hold great potential for engineering promising exciton phenomena, particularly interlayer excitons (IXs) featuring extended lifetimes and permanent out-of-plane electric dipole moments. While electrically controllable IX emission has been extensively explored in TMD heterobilayers, reconfiguring their band alignment to achieve selected exciton states and exploit these states for novel excitonic functionalities remains an urgent challenge. Here, we demonstrate dynamic exciton control by electrically tunable band alignment transitions between type-II and type-I configurations in WS2/(iso-BA)2PbI4 heterostructures, enabling reversible conversion between charged interlayer (IX±) and charged intralayer (X−) excitons. By tailoring these exciton states, we achieve two critical functionalities: (i) 7 μm ON/OFF control of exciton transport via transition between delocalized IX± (ON) and confined X− (OFF) states; (ii) valley polarization switching with a 16.3 ON/OFF ratio, leveraging distinct spin-valley configurations of IX± (unpolarized) and X− (polarized). Unlike twist-angle-dependent TMD heterobilayers, this platform operates independently of stacking alignment, establishing a broadly hybrid 2D system as a practical paradigm towards programmable nanophotonic circuits.
tldr: This paper demonstrates electrically tunable band alignment transitions in WS2/perovskite heterostructures to control exciton transport and valley polarization.
motivation: The authors aim to achieve dynamic control of exciton states in van der Waals heterostructures, enabling novel excitonic functionalities for nanophotonic circuits.
method: They fabricate WS2/(iso-BA)2PbI4 heterostructures and apply electric fields to switch between type-II and type-I band alignments, converting between charged interlayer and intralayer excitons.
result: They achieve 7 μm ON/OFF control of exciton transport and valley polarization switching with a 16.3 ON/OFF ratio.
conclusion: This platform offers a twist-angle-independent approach for programmable exciton control, potentially useful for nanophotonic devices.

title: Exploring Exotic Spin-dependent Interactions Beyond The Standard Model: Theoretical Foundations And Experimental Investigations
authors: L Y Wu And H Yan
abstract: New interactions mediated by novel particles propose solutions to several important questions in modern physics. Axions serve as examples of such particles; they are lightweight and interact weakly with ordinary matter. This category of particles, including those similar to axions—termed axion-like particles (ALPs)—arises from diverse theoretical frameworks, such as the Peccei-Quinn mechanism addressing the strong CP problem, string theory, and spontaneous supersymmetry breaking. Given their light mass and weak coupling, ALPs are also possible candidates for cold dark matter. Introducing these new interactions mediated by novel particles not only tackles several challenges in modern physics but also raises a crucial question: Are there undiscovered interactions beyond the standard model (SM)? Many of the interactions predicted by these theories are spin-dependent, which is the primary focus of this review. In this review, we first outline the theoretical foundations for investigating exotic spin-dependent interactions, highlighting their importance in various models beyond the SM. We examine the potential roles of new lightweight particles in mediating these interactions, which may enhance our understanding of dark matter. Relevant formulas derived from theoretical models are included to support experimental investigations. Following this theoretical framework, we conduct a detailed review of recent experimental efforts to detect these exotic interactions. A systematic review of current constraints on these interactions is presented, along with an assessment of various detection approaches.
tldr: This review explores exotic spin-dependent interactions beyond the Standard Model, focusing on axion-like particles and their experimental detection.
motivation: The paper aims to address open questions in modern physics, such as the strong CP problem and dark matter, by investigating new spin-dependent interactions mediated by novel particles.
method: The authors provide a theoretical overview of models predicting these interactions and then systematically review recent experimental efforts to detect them, including constraints and detection approaches.
result: The review compiles current experimental constraints on exotic spin-dependent interactions and assesses various detection methods.
conclusion: The paper serves as a comprehensive reference for the theoretical foundations and experimental status of exotic spin-dependent interactions, but it does not directly contribute to the user's specified research directions.

title: Non-spreading Meronic Spin Defects Around Optical Vortices
authors: Miguel A Porras And Yijie Shen Nilo Mata-Cervera
abstract: Optical vortices are singularity lines where the light field intensity vanishes and its phase is undefined. These threads of darkness are adorned by Gauss’s law as lines of pure longitudinal polarization where the polarization plane tilts and winds around. The resulting spin field is as a unique structure with both features of topological texture and defect, as it includes a point defect of undefined spin enclosed by a meronic texture which spans half the spin unit sphere. This topological structure does not spread in propagation: the normalized spin field maintains a deep-subwavelength confinement around the vortex line while the underlying vortex beam continues to diffract. From their intrinsic nature and subwavelength confinement, these textures exhibit enhanced robustness upon isotropic perturbations such as atmospheric turbulence compared with other tailored polarization textures. Here we describe these topologies of transverse spin which decorate the phase singularity of paraxial vortex beams, highlighting the diversity of topological structures that arise in two different spaces—the spin unit sphere and the transverse-axial Poincaré sphere—and discuss the underlying aspects behind their subwavelength localization.
tldr: This paper studies topological spin textures (meronic defects) around optical vortices, focusing on their subwavelength confinement and robustness to turbulence.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize novel topological structures in optical fields, specifically the spin textures that decorate phase singularities, and to explore their potential for robust light structuring.
method: They theoretically analyze the spin field of paraxial vortex beams, describing the meronic texture on the spin unit sphere and its relation to the transverse-axial Poincaré sphere, and compare robustness to perturbations.
result: They find that the normalized spin field maintains deep-subwavelength confinement and exhibits enhanced robustness to isotropic perturbations like atmospheric turbulence compared to other polarization textures.
conclusion: The work highlights a new class of topological spin defects in optics with potential applications in robust light structuring, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Multiphysics Tritium Transport Modelling Of The Arc Breeding Blanket With Festim
authors: James Dark, Arpan Sircar, Jin Whan Bae, J{\o}rgen S. Dokken, R\'emi Delaporte-Mathurin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate prediction of tritium behaviour in molten salt breeding blankets is essential for the design and safe operation of ARC-class fusion reactors. This work presents a fully open-source, component-scale multiphysics framework for modelling tritium transport in an ARC liquid immersion blanket. Neutron transport, thermal hydraulics, and hydrogen isotope transport are coupled using OpenMC, OpenFOAM, and FESTIM, leveraging dedicated tools enabling direct transfer of spatially resolved fields between solvers. Assuming a zero inlet concentration, steady-state simulations predict a total tritium inventory of approximately 243 mg, with the blanket reaching steady-state tritium throughput within approximately 30 min, which is of a similar order to previous system-level estimates. The results show that tritium transport is dominated by turbulence-enhanced diffusion, with strong localisation in flow stagnation regions and reduced accumulation in highly turbulent zones. Sensitivity analyses indicate that predicted inventories are governed primarily by the numerical stabilisation scheme, with only a modest dependence on the turbulent Schmidt number. The proposed workflow provides a transparent and extensible basis for high-fidelity analysis of tritium transport in ARC-class breeding blankets.
tldr: This paper presents a multiphysics simulation framework for tritium transport in a fusion breeding blanket, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Accurate prediction of tritium behavior is essential for the design and safety of fusion reactors, but this topic is outside the scope of the user's specified research directions.
method: The authors couple neutron transport (OpenMC), thermal hydraulics (OpenFOAM), and hydrogen isotope transport (FESTIM) in a component-scale model of an ARC liquid immersion blanket.
result: Steady-state simulations predict a total tritium inventory of ~243 mg, with steady-state throughput reached in ~30 min, and show that transport is dominated by turbulence-enhanced diffusion with sensitivity to numerical stabilization.
conclusion: The proposed workflow provides a transparent basis for tritium transport analysis in fusion blankets, but it has no connection to quantum information science or related fields.

title: Inverse Mask Design For Interference Lithography Using Automatic Differentiable Wave Propagation
authors: Chuntian Cao, Jangwoon Sung, Jack Griffiths, Yuan Gao, Xi Yu, Paul Baity, Nikhil Tiwale, Zhitian Shi, Juhong Ahn, Shinjae Yoo, Yong S. Chu, Chang-Yong Nam
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interference lithography (IL) is powerful for fabricating high-resolution periodic nanostructures, but designing masks to produce non-periodic patterns remains challenging. We introduce a gradient-based optimization framework for binary IL mask design using automatic differentiation. The forward model is implemented using the differentiable angular spectrum method (ASM). The inverse mask design is formulated as an optimization problem, where the mask logits are updated through backpropagation of the loss between the simulated field amplitude and the target pattern. We optimize a mask that reproduces a target pattern with only 0.1% isolated pixel-level defects, resolving features at half the mask pixel pitch. To scale mask optimization, we employ the shifted ASM, which partitions the mask into patches that are propagated independently and summed at the image plane. For a 3.84 mm[MATH]3.84 mm mask, shifted ASM with 16 patches reduces peak GPU memory by 3.8[MATH] at only 1.3[MATH] runtime cost relative to standard ASM. With gradient checkpointing, peak memory is reduced by 7.4[MATH] at 2[MATH] runtime. Distributing across multiple GPUs further accelerates the optimization. This work establishes a physics-informed, machine learning-driven approach for IL mask design, moving a step further towards complex, non-periodic patterns. The source code is available at [URL] .
tldr: This paper presents a gradient-based optimization framework for binary interference lithography mask design using automatic differentiation and differentiable angular spectrum method.
motivation: Interference lithography is powerful for periodic nanostructures, but designing masks for non-periodic patterns is challenging.
method: The authors formulate inverse mask design as an optimization problem, updating mask logits via backpropagation of the loss between simulated field amplitude and target pattern, and use shifted ASM for scalability.
result: The method achieves 0.1% pixel-level defects, resolves features at half the mask pixel pitch, and reduces GPU memory by up to 7.4x with gradient checkpointing.
conclusion: This work establishes a physics-informed, machine learning-driven approach for IL mask design, enabling complex non-periodic patterns.

title: Subexponential Bohnenblust-Hille Inequalities On Finite Cyclic Groups
authors: Anselmo Raposo Jr Daniel M. Pellegrino
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Slote, Volberg and Zhang proved a dimension-free Bohnenblust--Hille inequality on products of finite cyclic groups for functions of bounded total degree. Later, Becker, Klein, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proved [MATH] and asked whether the optimal constants are subexponential in the degree. More recently, Defant, Galicer, Mansilla, Masty\l o and Muro established an exponential Bohnenblust--Hille estimate for the larger support-sensitive class governed by the number of active coordinates. We prove that the optimal constants for this larger class grow subexponentially. More precisely, if [MATH] denotes the optimal constant for functions on [MATH] whose Fourier characters involve at most [MATH] coordinates, with no restriction on the nonzero local frequencies, then, for every fixed [MATH], \[ {q}\leq \exp\left(c_q +O_q\left(}\log\log d\right)\right) \qquad(d\to\infty), \] where [MATH] and [MATH] for [MATH]. motivation: The paper addresses an open question about optimal constants in Bohnenblust-Hille inequalities, which have applications in various areas of analysis.

title: The Hidden Life Of Public Safety Communications Signals: A Comparative Security Analysis Of Tetra, Tetrapol, And P25
authors: Sergey Bratus Larry Hernandez
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public-safety agencies and critical infrastructure operators rely on trunked land-mobile radio (LMR) systems, based on P25, TETRA, and TETRAPOL. These systems are expected to protect not just the content of a communication but the fact of it. Yet LMR standards leave a stark gap between confidentiality of and of : underneath an encrypted traffic plane, their signaling plane is almost entirely in the clear. We probe the depth and impact of adversarial inference from this exposed signaling. Prior security analyses of these systems have concentrated on the content plane---recovering encryption keys or capturing accidental cleartext. We show that comparably sensitive information can be . In particular, we show that across the trunked LMR standards, a passive, receive-only software-defined radio (SDR) observer can recover operationally sensitive network topology and geography details, unit presence, mobility across cells and groups, organizational structure, as well as operational security details such as special key domains and key-epoch rotation. This signaling-plane inference reaches far beyond the observer's direct area of reception, turning sniffing into network mapping capabilities that degrade or defeat LMR standards' identity obfuscation through timing and association. In the case of TETRAPOL, we demonstrate how inference and tracking of such signaling metadata and a standards-level confidentiality failure in emergency call handling enable unencrypted voice extraction. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and mitigations, including specific recommendations for protecting inter-cell, base station and subscriber identities.
tldr: This paper analyzes security vulnerabilities in public safety radio standards (TETRA, TETRAPOL, P25) by exploiting exposed signaling metadata to infer sensitive operational information.
motivation: Public safety agencies rely on these systems for confidentiality, but prior analyses focused on content encryption, leaving signaling-plane metadata unprotected and exploitable.
method: The authors conduct a comparative security analysis of the signaling planes of TETRA, TETRAPOL, and P25, demonstrating how a passive SDR observer can recover network topology, unit presence, and other operational details.
result: They show that signaling metadata can be used to map networks and track units, and in TETRAPOL, a confidentiality failure in emergency call handling enables unencrypted voice extraction.
conclusion: The paper recommends countermeasures to protect inter-cell, base station, and subscriber identities, highlighting the need for signaling-plane security in LMR systems.

title: Towards A Characterization Of Counting And Alternating Classes Via Discrete Ordinary Differential Equations
authors: Eduardo Skapinakis Melissa Antonelli
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a high-level report on an ongoing project aiming to leverage implicit approaches based on discrete ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to study multiple complexity classes, even beyond small circuit and polynomial-time classes. Stimulated by recent ODE-based characterizations of polynomial-time functions (FP) and classes over the reals, the research project outlined here pushes this investigation further into counting and alternation. Specifically, we present a uniform framework, built upon a single base algebra and a unified family of schemas, where complexity levels, such as those of the polynomial and counting hierarchies, are captured simply by the nesting depth of ODE operators. Crucially, our approach starts from a base class much weaker than FP, thus strengthening existing recursion-theoretic treatments and establishing a natural connection to descriptive complexity. Moreover, by isolating three elementary schemas, our framework makes the computational content of linearity restrictions completely transparent while extending ODE-based implicit complexity to previously unaddressed counting classes, such as oplusP. More generally, this work establishes a clear bridge between differentiation and counting, offering a fresh perspective on the relationships between different complexity classes, which remains the object of ongoing and future research.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework using discrete ordinary differential equations to characterize counting and alternating complexity classes, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The authors aim to extend implicit complexity approaches based on ODEs to counting and alternating classes, building on recent characterizations of polynomial-time functions.
method: They present a uniform framework with a single base algebra and a family of schemas, where complexity levels are captured by nesting depth of ODE operators, starting from a base class weaker than FP.
result: The framework captures polynomial and counting hierarchies, extends to classes like ⊕P, and clarifies the role of linearity restrictions.
conclusion: The work establishes a bridge between differentiation and counting, offering new perspectives on complexity class relationships, but it is purely theoretical computer science.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: This review covers the quantum-mechanical theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on tunneling, resonances, and interference effects.
motivation: Stellar nuclear reactions occur at low energies and are difficult to measure directly, so theoretical understanding is crucial for astrophysics.
method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches to low-energy nuclear reactions, including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference, and discusses new experimental ideas.
result: It summarizes the state of the art in theoretical nuclear astrophysics and highlights open challenges.

title: Competing Magnetic Order In EuPd 3 ...
authors: Michelle Ocker, Franziska Walther, Nour Maraytta, Matthieu Le Tacon, Michael Merz, Cornelius Krellner And Kristin Kliemt
abstract: Single crystals of EuPd Si were grown using a high-temperature EuPd-flux method. The material was structurally and chemically characterized by single-crystal x-ray diffraction, powder x-ray diffraction, Laue method and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy. The structural analysis confirmed the orthorhombic crystal structure (space group ) but revealed differences in the lattice parameters and bond distances. The composition is close to the ideal 1:3:2 stoichiometry with an occupation of 7% of the Si sites by Pd. The heat capacity, electrical resistivity, and magnetic susceptibility show two magnetic transitions indicating magnetic ordering below 61 K and a spin reorientation at 40 K. The orthorhombic material shows magnetic anisotropy, with anisotropy constants and , for field applied along the three main symmetry axes, which is summarized in the temperature-field phase diagrams. The susceptibility data hint to an alignment of the magnetic moments along between and . Below the magnetic structure changes to an arrangement with moments canted away from . The single crystals investigated in this study are suggested to show antiferromagnetic order below instead of ferromagnetism that sets in at higher which might originate from certain differences in the structure, composition or defects that have an impact on the dominant coupling constants of the Ruderman–Kittel–Kasuya–Yosida interaction.
tldr: This paper characterizes the structural and magnetic properties of EuPd3Si2 single crystals, focusing on competing magnetic orders and anisotropy.
motivation: To understand the magnetic behavior of EuPd3Si2, which may exhibit different magnetic ground states depending on structural details.
method: Single crystals were grown via flux method and characterized using X-ray diffraction, EDX, heat capacity, resistivity, and magnetization measurements.
result: Two magnetic transitions are observed at 61 K and 40 K, with anisotropic magnetic properties and a spin reorientation; the material shows antiferromagnetic order below 61 K.
conclusion: The magnetic order in EuPd3Si2 is sensitive to structural and compositional variations, affecting the dominant RKKY interactions.

title: Moiré-driven Skyrmion Family
authors: Kuan He, Meng-Han Li, Shi-Da Fan, Zi-Bin Lin, Xiao-Ying Zhuang, Cheng-Lin Han, Li-Qun Chen, Zhao-Dong Xu, Xue-Feng Zhu And Tian-Zhi Yang
abstract: Skyrmion family members, including skyrmions, merons, and skyrmioniums, have been observed in diverse physical systems, yet their coexistence and transformation within a single controllable platform remain challenging. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a bilayer twisted moiré elastic system that enables the generation of multiple skyrmion family members with different topological charges. By constructing three-dimensional displacement vector fields, we establish a framework describing the evolution of topological invariants under twist-induced symmetry modulation, thereby governing controlled transitions and the stable coexistence of different skyrmion textures. In addition, manipulating the Lamb-wave phase introduces discontinuous transport of the topological textures, thereby revealing phason-like dynamics within the quasiperiodic structure. Together, these results provide a versatile route for controlling topological textures and open new possibilities for the design of integrated topological wave devices.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a bilayer twisted moiré elastic system that generates and controls multiple skyrmion family members with different topological charges, revealing phason-like dynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to achieve coexistence and transformation of different skyrmion textures within a single controllable platform, which has been challenging.
method: They construct a bilayer twisted moiré elastic system and use three-dimensional displacement vector fields to describe topological invariant evolution under twist-induced symmetry modulation. They also manipulate Lamb-wave phase to induce discontinuous transport.
result: They experimentally demonstrate generation of multiple skyrmion family members with different topological charges and controlled transitions, as well as phason-like dynamics.
conclusion: The work provides a versatile route for controlling topological textures and opens possibilities for integrated topological wave devices.

title: Nucleation Beyond Equilibrium: Fronts Control Invasion In Bistable Ecosystems
authors: Victor Lequin, Giulio Biroli, Camille Scalliet
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bistability, the existence of two alternative stable states with distinct basins of attraction, is common across ecology and many other biological, chemical, and physical systems. In spatially extended systems, the invasion of one state by the other proceeds through nucleation, the fluctuation-driven growth of a droplet beyond a critical size. Classical Nucleation Theory (CNT) quantifies this process using the energy landscape, but this description relies on detailed balance, the condition of microscopic reversibility that holds at equilibrium. Ecological dynamics generally violate detailed balance and are described not by a single scalar field but by several coupled, non-conserved abundances--a vector order parameter--for which no general nucleation theory exists. Here we derive such a theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, valid both close to the binodal, where invasion proceeds through propagating fronts, and close to the spinodal, where the metastable state loses stability. Extensive numerical computations of the quasipotential confirm the theory in both regimes. We show that the mathematical structure of CNT survives out of equilibrium, once energetic quantities are replaced by dynamical properties of fronts: the front speed plays the role of the bulk free-energy difference between phases, and the diffusivity that of the surface tension. Applied to the two-species Lotka-Volterra model, an archetypal system of bistable ecological antagonism, our theory shows that strong interspecific competition generates a pronounced depletion region within fronts, where the total abundance falls well below carrying capacity. This vectorial structure, invisible to a scalar description based on species frequency alone, makes invasion exponentially harder as competition strengthens at fixed competitive advantage--a prediction testable in microbial systems.
tldr: This paper develops a nucleation theory for bistable ecosystems with non-conserved vector order parameters, showing that front dynamics control invasion beyond equilibrium.
motivation: Classical nucleation theory relies on detailed balance, which ecological systems violate; there is no general theory for vector order parameters.
method: The authors derive a theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, using quasipotential computations and front properties.
result: They show that front speed and diffusivity replace free-energy difference and surface tension, and that strong competition creates depletion regions making invasion exponentially harder.
conclusion: The theory extends nucleation concepts to non-equilibrium ecological systems and provides testable predictions for microbial systems.

title: Superfluid Helium

We present a mathematically solvable toy model of the phase transition between the normal liquid and superfluid phases and use it to show how an order parameter might be obtained for the superfluid.

method: They introduce a mathematically solvable toy model of the phase transition between normal liquid and superfluid phases.
